disease.name: Pyelonephritis (Kidney Infection)
disease.scientific_name: Pyelonephritis / Upper Urinary Tract Infection / Renal Parenchymal Infection
disease.icd_10_code: N10 (Acute pyelonephritis); N11.0 (Nonobstructive reflux-associated chronic pyelonephritis); N11.1 (Chronic obstructive pyelonephritis); N11.8 (Other chronic tubulo-interstitial nephritis); N13.6 (Pyonephrosis); O23.0 (Infections of kidney in pregnancy); N39.0 (Urinary tract infection, site not specified); N30.0 (Acute cystitis); A41.51 (Sepsis due to Escherichia coli — urosepsis); N15.1 (Renal and perinephric abscess)
disease.category: Infectious Disease / Urological / Nephrology / Public Health

overview.description: Pyelonephritis is a bacterial infection of the upper urinary tract — specifically involving the kidney parenchyma (renal tissue), collecting system (calyces), and renal pelvis. It most commonly arises from ascending spread of bacteria from the lower urinary tract (bladder — cystitis → ureter → kidney), though haematogenous spread (seeding of the kidney from bloodstream bacteraemia) also occurs. Pyelonephritis produces a systemic febrile illness with loin/flank pain, rigors, nausea and vomiting, and characteristic urinary symptoms, distinguishing it from uncomplicated lower UTI (cystitis) which causes only bladder irritation without systemic features. While most cases in otherwise healthy young women are uncomplicated and respond rapidly to oral antibiotics, pyelonephritis carries significant risk of life-threatening complications — including urosepsis, septic shock, renal abscess, and acute kidney injury — particularly in pregnant women, elderly patients, men, diabetics, and immunocompromised individuals. It accounts for over 100,000 hospital admissions annually in the USA alone and is the most common serious bacterial infection in women of reproductive age.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the kidneys (renal parenchyma, calyces, and renal pelvis); involvement may extend to the ureter, perinephric space (perinephric abscess), and systemically via bloodstream (bacteraemia and urosepsis)
overview.prevalence: Pyelonephritis affects approximately 1-2% of all UTI cases and accounts for up to 200,000 emergency department visits and 100,000 hospitalisations per year in the USA; global incidence estimated at 15-17 cases per 10,000 women per year; affects all age groups but peak incidence in women aged 15-35 years
overview.age_group: All ages; highest incidence in sexually active women aged 15-35 years; second peak in elderly over 65 years of both sexes; in children — important cause of febrile illness and a significant cause of renal scarring and chronic kidney disease
overview.is_contagious_note: Pyelonephritis itself is not contagious person-to-person; however, the causative bacteria (e.g., ESBL-producing E. coli) can be transmitted in healthcare settings through contaminated hands and equipment
overview.is_chronic_note: Acute pyelonephritis is not chronic; however, recurrent episodes cause renal scarring leading to chronic pyelonephritis and chronic kidney disease
overview.key_fact: Pyelonephritis is a medical emergency requiring same-day medical assessment — high fever with loin pain is never 'wait and see'; ESBL-producing E. coli is an emerging major problem in India making first-line oral antibiotic treatment increasingly unreliable

types.name: Uncomplicated Acute Pyelonephritis
types.description: Acute bacterial kidney infection occurring in an otherwise healthy, non-pregnant adult woman with a structurally and functionally normal urinary tract and no significant comorbidities. Uncomplicated pyelonephritis responds well to oral antibiotic therapy and is managed in the outpatient setting in the majority of cases. This is the most common clinical scenario — accounting for approximately 70-80% of all pyelonephritis cases.
types.typical_patient: Healthy, non-pregnant woman aged 18-50 years with no urological abnormalities, no recent hospitalisation, no catheter, no diabetes, and no immunosuppression
types.causative_organisms: E. coli (85-90% of cases in community setting)
types.management_setting: Outpatient oral antibiotics in most cases; hospital admission if vomiting prevents oral medication or features of systemic sepsis
types.prognosis: Excellent — fever resolves within 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics; full recovery expected within 10-14 days
types.recurrence_risk: 20-30% recurrence within 6 months in women with predisposing factors (sexual activity, prior UTI history)

types.name: Complicated Acute Pyelonephritis
types.description: Pyelonephritis occurring in the presence of structural, functional, or metabolic factors that increase the risk of a more severe course, treatment failure, antibiotic resistance, and complications. ANY of the following factors make pyelonephritis 'complicated' and necessitates a more aggressive management approach, including consideration of IV antibiotics and hospitalisation.
complicating_factors: Male sex — any UTI in men is considered complicated by definition (men should not normally develop UTIs without a predisposing cause)
Pregnancy — requires urgent treatment due to high risk of preterm labour, maternal sepsis, and foetal compromise
Urinary tract obstruction — urinary stone (calculus), stricture, or tumour obstructing urine flow; obstruction with infection creates pyonephrosis (pus in the collecting system) — SURGICAL EMERGENCY
Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) — abnormal retrograde flow of urine from bladder to ureter/kidney; particularly important in children
Diabetes mellitus — impaired neutrophil function; higher risk of emphysematous pyelonephritis and fungal infection
Immunosuppression — HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients, chemotherapy, high-dose corticosteroids
Urinary catheter (indwelling or intermittent) — catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI)
Recent urological instrumentation or surgery — increased risk of resistant organisms
Neurogenic bladder — incomplete bladder emptying promotes bacterial colonisation
Structural renal anomalies — horseshoe kidney, polycystic kidney disease, renal transplant
Renal impairment — reduced antibiotic clearance alters dosing; impaired immune defence
Recent hospitalisation or healthcare exposure — risk of ESBL-producing or multidrug-resistant organisms
Known MDR organism — ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae, carbapenem-resistant organisms
Failure of initial outpatient antibiotic therapy within 48-72 hours
types.management_setting: Hospital admission strongly recommended; IV antibiotics; imaging (renal ultrasound minimum, CT if complications suspected); urology referral if obstruction identified
types.prognosis: Variable — depends on underlying complicating factor and rapidity of treatment; mortality risk exists with urosepsis

types.name: Emphysematous Pyelonephritis (EPN)
types.description: A rare, life-threatening necrotising bacterial infection of the kidney parenchyma characterised by accumulation of gas within and around the kidney, produced by gas-forming bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis) fermenting glucose under anaerobic conditions. Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a urological and infectious disease emergency with mortality rates of 21-43% without aggressive surgical intervention.
types.epidemiology: Affects predominantly diabetics (90% of cases — poorly controlled blood glucose provides substrate for bacterial gas production); rare in non-diabetics (obstruction, immunosuppression); female:male ratio 3:1
types.organisms: E. coli (most common — 70%), Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus, Pseudomonas, occasionally mixed organisms; fungal (Candida) EPN in severely immunocompromised
types.clinical_features: Similar to severe pyelonephritis but typically more fulminant; may present in diabetic ketoacidosis; crepitus over kidney (rare but pathognomonic); gas on plain X-ray or CT scan
types.classification: Class I (gas in collecting system only — lower mortality); Class II (gas in renal parenchyma); Class IIIA (gas in perinephric space); Class IIIB (gas in pararenal space); Class IV (bilateral EPN or solitary kidney — highest mortality)
types.diagnosis: CT scan of abdomen (gold standard) — shows gas within kidney; X-ray may show renal gas (mottled appearance); avoid delay in diagnosis
types.management: ICU admission; urgent percutaneous drainage (preferred over open surgery for classes I-II); nephrectomy for extensive disease or failure to respond; IV antibiotics covering anaerobes (piperacillin-tazobactam or imipenem); intensive diabetes management; ICU haemodynamic support
types.mortality: 21-43% overall; highest in bilateral disease, thrombocytopenia, acute renal failure, and septic shock at presentation

types.name: Perinephric and Renal Abscess
types.description: A collection of pus within the renal parenchyma (intrarenal abscess) or in the perinephric space between the renal capsule and Gerota's fascia (perinephric abscess). Abscesses develop when pyelonephritis fails to resolve and bacteria localise and wall off, or when haematogenous seeding from distant infection (skin, teeth, endocarditis) reaches the kidney. Perinephric abscess is a serious complication requiring percutaneous or surgical drainage in addition to antibiotics.
types.causes: Ascending pyelonephritis failing to respond to antibiotics (most common); haematogenous spread from Staphylococcus aureus (skin, dental abscess, endocarditis); obstruction causing pus accumulation
types.organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus (ascending); Staphylococcus aureus (haematogenous — suggests distant focus of infection)
types.clinical_features: Fever persisting despite 5-7 days of appropriate antibiotics; palpable flank mass (large abscess); CVA tenderness; systemically unwell despite treatment; characteristic 'spiking' fever pattern (temperature swinging from normal to high)
types.diagnosis: Ultrasound (initial screen — may miss small abscesses); CT scan with contrast (gold standard — reveals collection, gas, and extent); guided drainage for culture and source control
types.management: IV antibiotics (prolonged — 4-6 weeks total); percutaneous CT-guided or ultrasound-guided drainage (primary treatment for abscesses >3-4 cm); surgical drainage or partial nephrectomy if percutaneous drainage fails; correct underlying cause (relieve obstruction, treat distant foci)

types.name: Chronic Pyelonephritis
types.description: A chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy resulting from repeated episodes of bacterial kidney infection causing progressive renal cortical scarring, parenchymal atrophy, and calyceal distortion. Unlike acute pyelonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis is not an active bacterial infection but rather the structural consequence of repeated or inadequately treated infections. It is a significant cause of chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease in both children and adults.
types.pathogenesis: Repeated acute pyelonephritis → neutrophil-mediated inflammation → fibrosis and scarring of renal papillae and cortex → calyceal clubbing and cortical thinning → progressive loss of nephrons → CKD
types.common_associations: Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) — particularly in children (reflux nephropathy is the childhood equivalent); recurrent UTIs with obstruction; infected renal stones (struvite calculi); inadequately treated acute pyelonephritis
types.clinical_features: Often asymptomatic until significant renal impairment occurs; may have recurrent UTIs; hypertension (very common — from renal scarring and renin-angiotensin system activation); proteinuria; elevated creatinine; anaemia of CKD; small shrunken kidneys with irregular cortical scarring on imaging
types.diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (small scarred kidneys with irregular outline); DMSA scintigraphy (gold standard for renal scar detection — shows photon-deficient areas); MCUG (micturating cystourethrogram — detects VUR in children); renal biopsy rarely needed
types.management: Treat and prevent recurrent UTIs; control hypertension (ACE inhibitors/ARBs — both antihypertensive and renoprotective); screen for and treat VUR (surgical or endoscopic ureteric reimplantation); monitor eGFR; nephrology referral for CKD management; renal replacement therapy (dialysis/transplant) if ESRD develops

types.name: Pyonephrosis
types.description: Infected hydronephrosis — a urological emergency in which the dilated obstructed renal collecting system is filled with purulent infected urine (pus). The combination of infection and obstruction prevents antibiotic penetration into the collecting system and promotes rapid renal destruction; bacteria and toxins enter the bloodstream causing rapidly progressive urosepsis that does not respond to antibiotics alone until the obstruction is relieved.
types.causes: Obstructing ureteric stone (most common); ureteric stricture; tumour compressing ureter; PUJ (pelviureteric junction) obstruction with superimposed infection
types.clinical_features: High fever, rigors, severe flank pain; systemically very unwell; signs of sepsis/shock; may have renal colic history; urine culture positive; kidney not decompressing with antibiotics alone
types.diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (dilated collecting system with echogenic contents — pus); CT IVU (confirms obstruction and identifies cause); urine culture and blood cultures positive
types.management: SURGICAL EMERGENCY — urgent ureteric drainage by retrograde ureteric stent (JJ stent insertion by urologist) or percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) under ultrasound guidance; IV antibiotics are adjunctive — drainage is the definitive treatment; ICU support for septic shock; definitive management of obstruction cause after acute phase (ureteroscopy for stone, ureteric surgery for stricture)
types.critical_note: Pyonephrosis is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY — antibiotics without drainage will fail; rapid progressive septic shock and death can occur without urological drainage intervention within hours

types.name: Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis (XGP)
types.description: A rare and unusual form of chronic granulomatous renal infection in which normal renal parenchyma is replaced by lipid-laden macrophages (xanthoma cells) and suppurative necrosis. XGP mimics renal carcinoma on imaging and is often discovered incidentally or at surgery. Associated with chronic obstruction (usually by a large staghorn calculus), recurrent infections, and impaired immune response.
types.epidemiology: Rare — fewer than 1 in 100,000; predominantly middle-aged women; strongly associated with Proteus mirabilis and E. coli infection with staghorn calculi; rare in children
types.clinical_features: Chronic ill health; recurrent UTIs; flank mass; weight loss; low-grade fever; renal function often preserved in the contralateral kidney; characteristic CT appearance — enlarged kidney with multiple hypodense masses replacing parenchyma with calculi
types.management: Almost always requires nephrectomy (simple or radical depending on extent); antibiotic preparation pre-operatively; laparoscopic or open surgical approach

severity_levels.name: Mild Acute Pyelonephritis
severity_levels.description: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a healthy non-pregnant adult woman with classical symptoms but without features of systemic sepsis, severe vomiting, or complications. Manageable in the outpatient setting.
severity_levels.criteria: Temperature <38.5°C or mild fever; mild to moderate loin pain; able to tolerate oral fluids and medications; no vomiting; haemodynamically stable (HR <100 bpm, BP normal); no complicating features (see TYPE-02); urine dipstick positive for infection
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unwell but able to manage oral medication at home with close telephone follow-up
severity_levels.management: Oral antibiotic therapy (ciprofloxacin or co-amoxiclav depending on local resistance patterns); adequate oral hydration (minimum 2-3L daily); paracetamol/ibuprofen for pain and fever; urine culture sent before antibiotics; GP review or urgent care clinic; telephone review at 24-48 hours; return to ED if not improving or worsening
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Not improving within 48-72 hours of antibiotics; temperature rising above 39°C; vomiting preventing oral medication; new or worsening systemic symptoms; pregnancy identified; urine culture showing resistant organism

severity_levels.name: Moderate Acute Pyelonephritis
severity_levels.description: Uncomplicated or early complicated pyelonephritis with significant systemic illness but without frank sepsis or shock. Requires hospital assessment, though may be managed with a short admission and step-down to oral antibiotics.
severity_levels.criteria: Temperature 38.5-39.5°C; significant loin pain; nausea with or without vomiting; heart rate 100-110 bpm; blood pressure maintained; no confusion; no hypotension; mildly elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 50-100 mg/L, WBC 12,000-18,000); complicating features present (pregnancy, diabetes, male, elderly) but haemodynamically stable
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to manage at home due to vomiting, high fever, or pain; requires IV fluids and parenteral antibiotics
severity_levels.management: Hospital admission for IV fluids (to correct dehydration and maintain urine output); IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone or gentamicin) until afebrile for 24 hours, then step-down to oral; antiemetics (ondansetron); blood cultures (x2 sets) before antibiotics; urine MC&S before antibiotics; monitoring of temperature, urine output, and renal function; renal ultrasound to exclude obstruction; step-down to oral antibiotics when tolerating; discharge with oral antibiotics to complete course
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: HR >110 bpm; BP falling; confusion; worsening renal function; rising CRP/WBC despite 48h antibiotics; imaging showing abscess, obstruction, or gas

severity_levels.name: Severe Pyelonephritis / Urosepsis
severity_levels.description: Pyelonephritis complicated by systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) meeting criteria for sepsis — a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to the kidney infection. The urinary tract is the most common source of Gram-negative bacteraemia. Urosepsis requires emergency assessment, aggressive IV antibiotics, IV fluid resuscitation, and ICU-level monitoring.
severity_levels.sepsis_criteria: Temperature >39.5°C or <36°C (hypothermia is an ominous sign); Heart rate >110-120 bpm; Respiratory rate >20 breaths/min; WBC >18,000/mcL or <4,000/mcL (leucopenia — very serious); Altered mental status (new confusion); Raised serum lactate >2 mmol/L (tissue hypoperfusion); Organ dysfunction — rising creatinine (AKI), falling urine output, deranged LFTs; Positive blood cultures (20-30% of hospitalised pyelonephritis)
severity_levels.functional_impact: Seriously unwell; emergency department or hospitalisation mandatory; high-dependency monitoring
severity_levels.management: Emergency department assessment; 'Sepsis Six' — give high-flow oxygen; take blood cultures; give IV antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation; give IV fluid bolus (500mL crystalloid); measure serum lactate; monitor urine output (catheterise if needed); urgent renal ultrasound to exclude obstruction; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem in high-resistance settings); haematology and microbiology input; ICU or HDU if haemodynamically unstable; source control (relieve obstruction — urology referral)
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Systolic BP <90 mmHg despite IV fluids; lactate >4 mmol/L; multi-organ failure — SEPTIC SHOCK

severity_levels.name: Septic Shock / Critical — Life-Threatening
severity_levels.description: The most severe manifestation of urosepsis — septic shock is defined as sepsis with haemodynamic failure: persistent hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg) despite adequate IV fluid resuscitation, requiring vasopressor therapy to maintain adequate tissue perfusion. Urinary source septic shock carries 15-30% mortality. Multi-organ failure may include acute kidney injury, respiratory failure (ARDS), hepatic dysfunction, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and cardiac dysfunction.
severity_levels.examples: Emphysematous pyelonephritis in diabetic with septic shock; pyonephrosis with obstructed infected kidney in elderly patient; perinephric abscess with bacteraemia and haemodynamic collapse; multidrug-resistant E. coli urosepsis in catheterised immunocompromised patient
severity_levels.management: ICU admission; vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line) to maintain MAP >65 mmHg; IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering MDR organisms (meropenem ± vancomycin); urgent source control — urology consultation for emergency drainage of obstruction or abscess; mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure; renal replacement therapy (CRRT) for severe AKI; haematology for DIC (FFP, platelets); continuous monitoring — arterial line, central venous line, urinary catheter; serial lactate measurements; strict fluid balance
severity_levels.mortality: 15-30% in septic shock from urinary source; higher with delayed antibiotics, obstruction not relieved, ESBL/MDR organisms, and elderly with multiple comorbidities

causative_organisms_overview.bacteria_ascending: Responsible for the vast majority of pyelonephritis cases (>95%); bacteria colonise the periurethral area and ascend via the urethra to bladder, then to kidney; E. coli is predominant in 80-85% of community-acquired cases
causative_organisms_overview.bacteria_haematogenous: Seeding of kidney from bacteraemia — particularly Staphylococcus aureus from skin infection, dental abscess, or endocarditis; accounts for 5-10% of cases
causative_organisms_overview.mdr_and_esbl: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producing Enterobacteriaceae increasingly prevalent — particularly in India, Southeast Asia, and hospital-acquired infections; resistant to most oral antibiotics including cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones; requires carbapenem treatment (ertapenem, meropenem)
causative_organisms_overview.fungi: Candida species — increasingly important in diabetics, immunocompromised, catheterised patients, and those on prolonged antibiotics; diagnosed by positive urine fungal culture

major_causative_organisms.virulence_factors: P-fimbriae (type 1 and P pili) — allows adhesion to uroepithelial cells; haemolysin (damages renal tubular cells); aerobactin (iron acquisition in kidney); capsular K antigen (resists phagocytosis); type 1 fimbriae bind to bladder urothelium. Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) strains are distinct from bowel E. coli.
major_causative_organisms.resistance_concern: ESBL-producing E. coli (CTX-M type) is a major and rapidly growing problem — resistant to cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, and often fluoroquinolones; sensitive only to carbapenems and nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin (only for cystitis — NOT pyelonephritis); increasingly prevalent in India (30-50% of UTI isolates in some centres)
major_causative_organisms.treatment: Susceptible strains: ciprofloxacin or co-trimoxazole; ESBL: ertapenem IV or meropenem IV

major_causative_organisms.features: Produces urease; associated with gas-forming infections (emphysematous pyelonephritis); can produce struvite/staghorn calculi; hypervirulent Klebsiella (hvKP) — liver abscess plus septic emboli to kidney (Klebsiella liver abscess syndrome — Asian populations)
major_causative_organisms.resistance_concern: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) producing KPC, NDM, or OXA-48 — pan-drug resistant strains are emerging; major hospital-acquired pathogen
major_causative_organisms.treatment: Susceptible: ceftriaxone; ESBL: carbapenems; CRKP: colistin, fosfomycin combinations (limited options)

major_causative_organisms.proportion: 5% of community-acquired; higher in catheterised patients and urinary stones
major_causative_organisms.features: Produces urease — splits urea to ammonia and CO2 — alkalinises urine (pH >7) → precipitates magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite stones / staghorn calculi); associated with recurrent UTIs and chronic obstructive pyelonephritis; produces NH3 that is directly nephrotoxic; flagella and swarming motility facilitate ascending infection
major_causative_organisms.treatment: Co-amoxiclav; cephalosporins; resistance to nitrofurantoin; treat associated stones (urease-splitting stone removal essential to eradicate infection)

major_causative_organisms.proportion: 5-10%; common in nosocomial (hospital-acquired) UTI and in urological patients
major_causative_organisms.features: NOT covered by cephalosporins — important gap; amoxicillin-susceptible in most community strains; VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococcus) is emerging nosocomial concern
major_causative_organisms.treatment: Amoxicillin/ampicillin for susceptible strains; vancomycin for penicillin-allergic; linezolid for VRE

major_causative_organisms.proportion: 5-15% of UTI in sexually active young women specifically; less common than in cystitis
major_causative_organisms.features: Urease-producing; naturally resistant to nalidixic acid; found predominantly in young sexually active women (associated with sexual activity)

major_causative_organisms.proportion: Uncommon in community; common in hospital-acquired, catheter-associated, and recurrent UTI in structural abnormalities
major_causative_organisms.features: Intrinsically resistant to most first-line antibiotics; requires anti-pseudomonal cover (piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, ciprofloxacin — if susceptible, meropenem)
major_causative_organisms.treatment: Piperacillin-tazobactam; ceftazidime; ciprofloxacin (if susceptible); meropenem for MDR strains; combination therapy for severe infection

major_causative_organisms.proportion: Important specifically in pregnancy and elderly diabetics
major_causative_organisms.features: Normal lower GI and vaginal flora — becomes pathogenic in pregnancy; can cause maternal pyelonephritis and neonatal sepsis/meningitis if untreated in pregnancy

major_causative_organisms.proportion: Uncommon; seen in diabetics, immunocompromised, catheterised, post-antibiotics, ICU patients
major_causative_organisms.features: Yeast forms in urine; can form fungal balls obstructing collecting system; diagnose by urine microscopy (budding yeast, pseudohyphae) and fungal culture
major_causative_organisms.treatment: Fluconazole (most Candida albicans); voriconazole; amphotericin B for fluconazole-resistant species

routes_of_infection.description: Bacteria from the periurethral area (normal bowel flora contaminating the perineum) colonise the urethra → ascend to the bladder (cystitis) → ascend via the ureter → reach the renal pelvis and parenchyma (pyelonephritis). The relatively short female urethra (3-4 cm vs male 20 cm) explains the dramatically higher incidence of UTI in women. Uropathogenic E. coli have specific virulence factors (pili) enabling them to adhere to urothelium and resist washout by urinary flow.
facilitating_factors: Sexual intercourse — 'milks' bacteria into the urethra (honeymoon cystitis)
Use of spermicides and diaphragm — alters vaginal flora (kills Lactobacillus — the protective flora — and favours E. coli colonisation)
Urinary catheterisation — direct pathway for bacteria to enter bladder
Incomplete bladder emptying — stasis allows bacterial multiplication
Urinary tract obstruction — impairs clearance of bacteria by urine flow

routes_of_infection.description: Bacteria from a distant primary focus of infection seed the kidney via the bloodstream. Less common than ascending route. The kidney's rich blood supply makes it vulnerable to haematogenous seeding during bacteraemia.
sources: Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia from skin infection, wound infection, or endocarditis
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (renal TB — haematogenous spread from primary pulmonary TB)
Salmonella typhi bacteraemia seeding to kidney
Fungaemia — Candida in immunocompromised or IV drug users

routes_of_infection.description: Direct spread from adjacent infected structures — e.g., ascending cholangitis or appendiceal abscess tracking to perinephric space; extremely uncommon.

risk_factors: Female sex — short urethra (3-4 cm vs 20 cm in males); proximity of urethra to anus and vagina; post-menopausal oestrogen deficiency reduces uroepithelial Lactobacillus protection
Sexual activity — especially new or frequent partner; intercourse 'milks' bacteria into urethra; diaphragm and spermicide use significantly increase risk
Prior UTI history — strongest single risk factor for recurrent UTIs; previous pyelonephritis significantly increases risk of further episodes

Pregnancy — ureteral dilation from progesterone and mechanical compression reduce urine flow; immunological changes; asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy has 30% progression to pyelonephritis if untreated

Diabetes mellitus — impaired neutrophil chemotaxis, adherence, and killing; glucosuria provides bacterial nutrient; autonomic neuropathy impairs bladder emptying; high risk of emphysematous pyelonephritis
Urinary tract obstruction — kidney or ureteric stones (nephrolithiasis), strictures, BPH, pelvic masses, retroperitoneal fibrosis; obstruction impairs urine clearance of bacteria
Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) — particularly in children and young women; allows infected bladder urine to reach kidney
Urinary catheterisation — indwelling catheters cause CAUTI within 24-72 hours; risk increases 5-10% per day of catheter in situ
Urological instrumentation — cystoscopy, ureteroscopy, nephrostomy, lithotripsy; disrupts protective barriers
Renal and urinary tract structural abnormalities — horseshoe kidney, duplex collecting system, polycystic kidneys, ureterocele
Immunosuppression — HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200), post-transplant immunosuppressants, chemotherapy, high-dose corticosteroids, biologic therapies
Neurogenic bladder — spinal cord injury, MS, diabetic cystopathy, post-pelvic surgery; incomplete emptying and catheter use
Recent antibiotic use — disrupts vaginal and periurethral Lactobacillus flora; selects resistant organisms
Male with any UTI — must investigate underlying cause (BPH, prostatitis, structural abnormality); UTI is not 'normal' in men
Constipation — increases periurethral faecal colonisation; particularly in children
Post-menopausal status — oestrogen deficiency causes atrophy of vaginal and periurethral mucosa; loss of protective Lactobacillus flora
Blood group P1 — P-fimbriated E. coli bind P blood group antigen on uroepithelium; genetic susceptibility to recurrent UTI

symptoms.overview: Pyelonephritis presents as a systemic febrile illness with upper urinary tract involvement — distinguishing it from uncomplicated lower UTI (cystitis) which causes only bladder irritation without systemic features. The classic triad is fever/rigors + loin pain + lower urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency). However, not all three components are always present, and elderly patients may present atypically with confusion, vague malaise, or falls without localising urinary symptoms. Rapid clinical deterioration to sepsis can occur within hours in complicated cases.

primary_symptoms.name: Fever and Rigors
primary_symptoms.description: High fever (typically 38.5-40°C) is the hallmark of pyelonephritis and distinguishes it from cystitis (which does not cause significant fever). Onset is often abrupt — patients may describe being well and then feeling suddenly unwell within hours. Rigors (uncontrollable shivering episodes with extreme chills, lasting 15-30 minutes, followed by drenching sweats) indicate bacteraemia — bacteria have entered the bloodstream from the infected kidney. Rigors are an important warning sign of serious systemic infection and mandate blood cultures and IV antibiotics.
primary_symptoms.onset: Acute — often within hours; high fever and rigors may precede urinary symptoms
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Fever persisting beyond 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics suggests: wrong antibiotic, resistant organism, abscess formation, obstruction, or alternative diagnosis — MUST investigate with imaging

primary_symptoms.name: Loin Pain / Flank Pain (Costovertebral Angle Tenderness — CVA Tenderness)
primary_symptoms.description: Pain and tenderness in the loin (flank region — between the 12th rib and the iliac crest, lateral to the paraspinal muscles). Characteristically unilateral, though bilateral infection occurs. The pain may radiate anteriorly to the ipsilateral iliac fossa or groin. On physical examination, CVA tenderness (costovertebral angle tenderness) — elicited by gentle percussion of the costovertebral angle — is the most important clinical sign of pyelonephritis; a patient who recoils from this sign almost certainly has upper tract involvement. Deep palpation may reveal a tender, enlarged kidney.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Severe — can be debilitating
primary_symptoms.onset: Often comes on over hours to a day; can be sudden in pyonephrosis or renal abscess
primary_symptoms.note: Distinguish from musculoskeletal back pain (no fever, no urinary symptoms, related to movement/position) and renal colic (colicky pain radiating to groin with haematuria, no high fever unless infected stone)

primary_symptoms.name: Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS) — Dysuria, Frequency, Urgency
primary_symptoms.description: Symptoms of bladder irritation — burning pain on passing urine (dysuria), needing to urinate more frequently than normal (frequency), and urgent inability to defer voiding (urgency) — are present in approximately 60-70% of pyelonephritis cases. These reflect coexisting or antecedent cystitis (lower UTI that has ascended to involve the kidney). Their presence in combination with fever and loin pain strongly supports the diagnosis. However, LUTS may be absent in 30-40% of patients with pyelonephritis — particularly in those with haematogenous infection, the elderly, and catheterised patients.
primary_symptoms.onset: LUTS often precede the onset of fever and loin pain by 24-48 hours — this timeline suggests ascending spread

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea, Vomiting, and Anorexia
primary_symptoms.description: Nausea and vomiting occur in approximately 50-70% of patients with pyelonephritis — caused by both the systemic inflammatory response (cytokine-mediated) and sympathetic nervous system activation from renal capsule stretching. Vomiting preventing adequate oral fluid intake and medication administration is a key indication for hospital admission and IV therapy. Anorexia (loss of appetite) is universal in moderate-to-severe disease.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Persistent vomiting preventing oral antibiotics and fluids = mandatory hospital admission for IV therapy

primary_symptoms.name: Systemic Sepsis Features
primary_symptoms.description: In severe pyelonephritis progressing to urosepsis, systemic features of sepsis develop: tachycardia (heart rate >100 bpm), tachypnoea (respiratory rate >20/min), hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg in septic shock), confusion or altered consciousness (reduced cerebral perfusion and cytokine-mediated encephalopathy), cold clammy peripheries (peripheral vasoconstriction), and in extreme cases mottled skin and central cyanosis (cardiovascular collapse).
primary_symptoms.onset: Can develop rapidly — within hours of initial presentation; particularly in elderly and diabetic patients who may decompensate quickly
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: ANY of: confusion, heart rate >120, SBP <90, RR >25, or temperature >40°C or <36°C = SEPSIS — immediate IV antibiotics and resuscitation required

primary_symptoms.name: Cloudy/Offensive Urine and Haematuria
primary_symptoms.description: Cloudy urine (pyuria — white blood cells in urine making it turbid) and offensive/foul-smelling urine from bacterial metabolism are very common presenting features. Haematuria (blood in urine) occurs in approximately 40% of cases — typically microscopic (detected on dipstick) though gross haematuria (visibly red or pink urine) is also seen. Haematuria with flank pain and fever distinguishes infected stones (calculi) from simple pyelonephritis — must be differentiated by imaging.
primary_symptoms.onset: Often the first symptom noticed by patients

secondary_symptoms: Headache — from fever and systemic inflammatory response; dehydration-related
Generalised myalgia (muscle aches) — from systemic cytokine release (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1)
Malaise and fatigue — universal with pyelonephritis; can persist for 2-4 weeks after infection resolves
Abdominal pain — anterior radiation of loin pain; may mimic appendicitis (right-sided) or ovarian pathology in women; ileus in severe sepsis
Urinary frequency at night (nocturia) — bladder irritation from ongoing infection
Lower abdominal discomfort — suprapubic pain from coexisting cystitis
Dark concentrated urine — from reduced fluid intake and high insensible losses from fever
Joint pains and arthralgia — systemic inflammatory response
Low back pain — from renal involvement and referred pain from kidney capsule distension
Hypotension (postural dizziness) — from dehydration; sinister if at rest (sepsis)

atypical_presentations.features: Frequently atypical — may have NO fever (immunosenescence impairs fever response), NO loin pain, and NO dysuria; presents instead as: confusion and acute delirium, falls, reduced mobility, anorexia and general malaise, urinary incontinence (new or worsening), hypothermia (very serious), or vague deterioration in function. Pyelonephritis is one of the most common causes of acute confusion (delirium) in the elderly — always check urinalysis and MSU in any acutely confused elderly patient
atypical_presentations.warning: Elderly patients with pyelonephritis may appear deceptively well despite severe systemic infection — do not be falsely reassured by absence of fever

atypical_presentations.features: Non-specific — fever (often the only sign), poor feeding, irritability, weight loss, vomiting, jaundice (neonates), failure to thrive; UTI and pyelonephritis should be suspected in any febrile infant without obvious source — urine culture essential in all febrile infants

Abdominal pain (often periumbilical — not always flank pain), fever, vomiting, dysuria/frequency may be absent in younger children; bed-wetting (secondary enuresis) may be presenting symptom; rule out vesicoureteric reflux with MCUG imaging after first UTI in boys or second UTI in girls

Typically symptomatic — flank pain and fever; however, may have asymptomatic bacteriuria which has a 30% risk of progressing to pyelonephritis if untreated; any UTI symptoms in pregnancy must be assessed urgently; right-sided pain predominates (uterus displaces right ureter); Group B Streptococcus is a particularly important pathogen
Attenuated fever response; lack of classical symptoms; rapid progression to sepsis; unusual organisms (fungal, Mycobacterium, CMV); may be afebrile despite bacteraemia

Urine always cloudy and bacteriuric with catheter — bacteriuria alone does NOT mean infection; only treat CAUTI if symptomatic (fever, new confusion, loin pain, haemodynamic instability) or pre-operatively; asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterised patients should NOT be treated with antibiotics (promotes resistance)

warning_signs_of_serious_disease: Rigors (uncontrollable violent shivering) — bacteraemia; must have blood cultures and IV antibiotics immediately
Confusion or altered mental status — urosepsis with cerebral involvement; EMERGENCY
Heart rate above 110-120 bpm with hypotension or near-fainting — sepsis/septic shock
Temperature above 40°C or below 36°C (hypothermia — very ominous sign) — severe sepsis
No urine output or less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour despite adequate fluids — AKI or obstruction
Fever not improving or worsening after 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics — consider abscess, obstruction, resistant organism — URGENT IMAGING
Flank pain radiating to groin with haematuria — may indicate obstructing stone with infection; pyonephrosis risk — URGENT UROLOGY REFERRAL
Palpable tender flank mass — possible renal or perinephric abscess
Diabetic patient presenting with severe pyelonephritis features — high risk emphysematous pyelonephritis; CT scan urgently
Pregnant woman with any UTI symptoms — urgent assessment; high risk of preterm labour and maternal sepsis

medical_history: Duration of symptoms — fever onset, loin pain onset, urinary symptoms; rate of progression
Urinary symptoms — dysuria (burning on urination), urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, haematuria, cloudy or offensive urine
Systemic symptoms — fever severity, rigors, nausea/vomiting, anorexia, confusion, back pain
Previous UTI history — frequency, which organisms, which antibiotics used, response to treatment; prior pyelonephritis episodes
Renal stone history — previous nephrolithiasis, stone passage, lithotripsy; colicky flank pain radiating to groin
Urological history — previous urological surgery, catheterisation, cystoscopy, ureteroscopy, nephrostomy; structural abnormalities known
Pregnancy status — last menstrual period; urine pregnancy test in all women of reproductive age; specific risk in all trimesters

Sexual history — recent sexual activity; new partner; contraceptive method (diaphragm and spermicides increase risk; oral contraceptive pill does not increase risk); risk of sexually transmitted infection (co-infection with Chlamydia, Gonorrhoea)
Diabetes — known diabetes, blood glucose control, HbA1c; high risk of emphysematous pyelonephritis
Immunosuppression — HIV status, organ transplant, chemotherapy, high-dose steroids, biologic therapies
Recent hospitalisation or healthcare exposure — risk of MDR/ESBL organism
Recent antibiotic use — which antibiotics, duration, for what indication; prior ESBL isolate
Fluid intake — adequate hydration; history of dehydration
Catheter in situ — type, duration, last change
Family history — polycystic kidney disease; VUR; recurrent UTIs
Current medications — immunosuppressants, steroids, chemotherapy, diuretics; anticoagulants (relevant for procedural risk)
physical_examination: Vital signs — temperature (fever >38°C significant; hypothermia <36°C is very serious — sepsis); heart rate (tachycardia >100 bpm); blood pressure (hypotension <90/60 = shock); respiratory rate (tachypnoea >20/min = sepsis); oxygen saturation; urine output assessment
General appearance — does the patient look unwell? (toxic vs comfortable); pallor; diaphoresis (sweating); jaundice (rare — sepsis-related liver dysfunction)
Hydration status — skin turgor, mucous membranes, capillary refill time, blood pressure lying and standing (postural hypotension indicates dehydration)

Abdominal examination — inspection for distension; auscultation (bowel sounds); palpation for anterior renal tenderness, suprapubic tenderness (cystitis), flank mass (abscess); guarding or rigidity (rare — suggests peritoneal involvement from rupture)

Costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness — the key physical sign of pyelonephritis; performed by placing one hand flat over the costovertebral angle (junction of 12th rib and paraspinal muscles) and striking it with a closed fist (kidney punch test); sharp tender recoil = CVA tenderness positive — highly suggestive of pyelonephritis; must be bilateral to compare sides
Palpation of kidneys — bimanual ballottement of each kidney; enlarged or tender kidney; palpable perinephric mass

External genitalia examination where appropriate — discharge suggesting STI; vulvovaginitis in women; prostate tenderness on rectal examination in men (prostatitis — bimanual rectal examination; if prostatitis suspected do NOT vigourously massage prostate — risks bacteraemia)
Neurological assessment — confusion, altered consciousness, signs of meningism (rare — haematogenous meningitis with E. coli in neonates)
Skin — peripheral cyanosis, mottling (signs of poor perfusion in septic shock); no specific rash in pyelonephritis
Lower limb oedema — relevant to overall fluid status and CKD assessment

diagnostic_tests.description: The immediate, rapid, and most important initial investigation. Detects chemical markers of urinary infection within 60-90 seconds. Leucocyte esterase (released by white blood cells in urine) and nitrites (produced by Gram-negative bacteria reducing dietary nitrates to nitrites via nitrate reductase) are the key markers. Combined positive leucocyte esterase AND nitrites has approximately 90% sensitivity for significant bacteriuria. A negative dipstick (both nitrites and leucocyte esterase negative) makes significant UTI unlikely in uncomplicated cases.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid bedside detection of pyuria and bacteriuria; guide need for urine culture; triage severity
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Leucocyte esterase ++ or +++ = significant pyuria; Nitrites positive = Gram-negative bacteriuria (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus); Blood: haematuria (common); Protein: from inflammation and renal involvement
diagnostic_tests.limitations: False negatives with: Gram-positive organisms (Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus — do not reduce nitrates to nitrites — negative nitrites despite infection); very dilute urine (<first morning void); very recent UTI onset (bacteria not enough time to reduce nitrates); false positives: contaminated samples; vaginal leucocytes; dipstick deterioration; NEVER treat solely on a positive dipstick without culture if symptoms are atypical

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Midstream Urine (MSU) Culture and Sensitivity — Urine MC&S
diagnostic_tests.description: The gold standard investigation for urinary tract infection. A midstream clean-catch urine sample is sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity testing. Microscopy: WBCs (>5-10/HPF = pyuria); red blood cells; bacteria; WBC CASTS (clumps of WBCs shaped by the renal tubule — PATHOGNOMONIC of pyelonephritis vs simple cystitis — indicates kidney involvement). Culture: identifies causative organism after incubation for 24-48 hours. Sensitivity: determines antibiotic susceptibilities to guide targeted treatment.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm infection; identify specific causative organism; determine antibiotic susceptibility; guide antibiotic choice (targeted vs empirical); detect resistant organisms (ESBL, CRKP)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Significant bacteriuria: >10^5 colony-forming units (CFU) per mL in a clean-catch midstream specimen; >10^3 CFU/mL in catheter samples; WBC casts on microscopy = pyelonephritis; Sensitivity results guide antibiotic choice (susceptible S, intermediate I, resistant R)
diagnostic_tests.collection_technique: MSU — midstream clean-catch technique: women: clean labia with antiseptic wipe, pass initial urine stream, collect mid-portion into sterile container; men: retract foreskin if uncircumcised, clean glans, collect midstream portion. Catheter specimen: aspirate from sampling port using sterile needle and syringe (NOT from drainage bag). Process within 2 hours of collection or refrigerate at 4°C.
diagnostic_tests.timing: MUST BE SENT BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS — culture yields drop significantly after even one dose of antibiotics; if antibiotics must start immediately (severe sepsis), draw blood cultures and catheter sample simultaneously, then start antibiotics within 1 hour
diagnostic_tests.note: Results take 24-72 hours — empirical antibiotic therapy is started immediately based on clinical presentation and local resistance patterns, then adjusted (de-escalated or escalated) when sensitivity results available

diagnostic_tests.description: Phase-contrast or standard light microscopy of freshly centrifuged urine. WBC casts (cylindrical structures formed when WBCs are trapped in protein matrix within the renal tubular lumen) are PATHOGNOMONIC of renal parenchymal inflammation — distinguishing pyelonephritis from cystitis. Their presence in a febrile patient with loin pain confirms upper urinary tract involvement.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm pyelonephritis vs cystitis; detect RBC casts (renal glomerular bleeding vs lower tract); identify bacteria and yeast
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC casts = pyelonephritis (pathognomonic); RBC casts = glomerulonephritis; granular/waxy casts = chronic kidney disease; >10 WBC/hpf = significant pyuria

diagnostic_tests.description: Two sets of blood cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) taken from different venepuncture sites before initiating antibiotics. Approximately 20-30% of hospitalised pyelonephritis patients are bacteraemic. Blood cultures are essential for: confirming the causative organism (may not grow in urine if patient already on antibiotics); detecting bacteraemia that changes management; establishing antibiotic sensitivities; public health surveillance of resistant organisms.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect bacteraemia; guide targeted antibiotic therapy; detect MDR/ESBL organisms; public health surveillance
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive in 20-30% of hospitalised pyelonephritis; Gram-negative bacteraemia (E. coli, Klebsiella) most common; result in 24-72 hours
diagnostic_tests.indication: ALL hospitalised pyelonephritis; rigors; fever >39°C; signs of sepsis; immunocompromised patients; diabetics; elderly with suspected pyelonephritis
diagnostic_tests.note: Take blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics — cultures are often negative if even one dose of antibiotics given first; in septic shock, blood cultures should be drawn within minutes of presentation before antibiotic administration

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) / Complete Blood Count
diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated white blood cell count (leucocytosis) with neutrophilia confirms significant systemic bacterial infection. The WBC count in pyelonephritis typically ranges from 12,000-25,000/mcL with neutrophil predominance. Severe leucopenia (WBC <4,000/mcL) in pyelonephritis is an ominous sign suggesting severe sepsis with bone marrow suppression or very high bacterial load. Anaemia (normochromic normocytic — of chronic disease) may be present in recurrent or chronic disease.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm bacterial infection severity; guide antibiotic and admission decisions; detect leucopenia (sepsis severity marker); baseline for monitoring
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC >12,000 with neutrophilia (>75% neutrophils, band forms) = significant bacterial infection; WBC >20,000 = severe infection; WBC <4,000 = leucopenia — serious sign of severe sepsis; platelets falling = DIC in septic shock

diagnostic_tests.description: CRP is a hepatic acute phase reactant — rises within 6-12 hours of infection onset, peaks at 24-48 hours. In pyelonephritis, CRP is typically markedly elevated (>100 mg/L) and distinguishes upper UTI from cystitis (CRP usually <10-20 mg/L in cystitis). Serial CRP measurements monitor treatment response — falling CRP at 48-72 hours confirms clinical improvement. Procalcitonin (PCT) is more specific for bacterial sepsis — rises rapidly in bacteraemia and urosepsis; PCT >2 ng/mL indicates systemic bacterial infection; PCT-guided antibiotic stewardship reduces unnecessary antibiotic courses.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm significant upper tract infection (vs cystitis); monitor treatment response; guide antibiotic stewardship; predict bacteraemia risk
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CRP <20: likely cystitis; CRP 50-100: significant upper UTI; CRP >100: severe infection likely; PCT >0.5 ng/mL: suggests bacteraemia; PCT >2 ng/mL: bacterial sepsis very likely

diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in all hospitalised patients with pyelonephritis. Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in 10-20% of hospitalised pyelonephritis — from a combination of cytokine-mediated renal vasoconstriction, direct bacterial nephrotoxicity, and sepsis-related hypoperfusion. Rising serum creatinine and falling eGFR indicate AKI. Electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia) occur from vomiting, reduced intake, and sepsis-mediated fluid shifts. Hyperkalaemia indicates severe AKI — risk of fatal arrhythmia.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect AKI (rising creatinine); assess severity of renal impairment; guide antibiotic dosing (renally excreted antibiotics require dose adjustment in AKI); detect electrolyte imbalances; guide IV fluid composition and volume
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Creatinine rising above baseline = AKI; creatinine >200 mcmol/L = significant AKI requiring renal monitoring; hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L = emergency

diagnostic_tests.description: Blood glucose must be measured in all patients with pyelonephritis — undiagnosed diabetes is common in patients presenting with pyelonephritis (UTI may be the presentation of new diabetes). Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function and promotes bacterial growth. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) can be precipitated by pyelonephritis in diabetics — glucose and ketone measurement is essential in sick diabetics. HbA1c provides medium-term glucose control assessment and predicts risk of recurrent infections.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for new diabetes; assess glycaemic control (risk factor for recurrence and severe disease); detect DKA; guide management of diabetic pyelonephritis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Blood glucose >11.1 mmol/L (random) or >7.0 mmol/L (fasting) = diabetes; HbA1c >48 mmol/mol (6.5%) = diabetes diagnosis; ketones positive = DKA risk

diagnostic_tests.description: Serum lactate is a key biomarker of tissue hypoperfusion in sepsis — elevated when oxygen delivery to tissues is insufficient (anaerobic metabolism produces lactic acid). Serum lactate is used in the Sepsis-3 definition and in the 'Sepsis Six' resuscitation bundle. In pyelonephritis, elevated lactate indicates significant tissue hypoperfusion even when blood pressure appears relatively normal (cryptic shock). Serial lactate measurements guide fluid resuscitation response.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for occult sepsis and tissue hypoperfusion; guide resuscitation in sepsis; predict mortality risk
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Lactate <2 mmol/L: normal; Lactate 2-4 mmol/L: elevated — significant hypoperfusion; Lactate >4 mmol/L: severe tissue hypoperfusion / septic shock — high mortality risk

diagnostic_tests.description: A urine or blood pregnancy test must be performed in ALL women of reproductive age presenting with pyelonephritis — pregnancy changes management significantly (antibiotic choice, admission thresholds, imaging approach, dose modifications). Pyelonephritis in pregnancy is a medical emergency requiring hospitalisation in most cases.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect pregnancy before antibiotic prescribing (antibiotic safety differs in pregnancy); alter management threshold; guide imaging decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive hCG = pregnancy; ensure pregnancy-safe antibiotic (amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefalexin, ceftriaxone — safe; avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides in first/second trimester; avoid trimethoprim in first trimester, nitrofurantoin at term)

diagnostic_tests.description: The first-line imaging investigation in pyelonephritis — safe (no radiation), widely available, rapid, and relatively inexpensive. Ultrasound can identify: hydronephrosis/hydroureter (obstruction — dilated collecting system), renal calculi (echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing), renal or perinephric abscess (hypoechoic collection), enlarged kidney (acute inflammation), impaired corticomedullary differentiation, and complications such as pyonephrosis. Ultrasound should be performed urgently in all hospitalised patients with pyelonephritis and in any patient not responding to 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude obstruction (urgent — obstruction with infection = emergency); detect abscess; identify calculi; assess renal size and parenchyma; guide percutaneous drainage
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Dilated collecting system (pelviectasis, hydroureter) = obstruction — URGENT UROLOGY REFERRAL; focal hypoechoic area = abscess; echogenic foci with shadowing = calculus; enlarged oedematous kidney = acute pyelonephritis
diagnostic_tests.indication: All hospitalised patients; failure to improve within 48-72 hours; male patients (all); suspected obstruction; diabetes; immunocompromised; pregnancy
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Limited by bowel gas and patient body habitus; CT is more sensitive for small stones, gas, and early abscess

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CT Scan of Abdomen and Pelvis (with and without contrast — CT IVU/CT KUB)
diagnostic_tests.description: The gold standard imaging investigation for complicated pyelonephritis. CT provides detailed anatomical information unachievable with ultrasound: identifies obstruction and its cause (stone, mass, stricture); detects early parenchymal changes of pyelonephritis (striated nephrogram, focal oedema, abscesses); diagnoses emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas within or around kidney — visible on CT before X-ray); detects small perinephric collections; images ureteral course in full; provides roadmap for drainage or surgery.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose complications of pyelonephritis (abscess, EPN, obstruction); evaluate for urological cause; investigate failure to respond to antibiotics; pre-procedure planning
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Striated or focal nephrogram = acute pyelonephritis; gas within kidney = emphysematous pyelonephritis; focal hypodense area with rim enhancement = abscess; dilated collecting system with delayed excretion = obstruction; calculus = stone
diagnostic_tests.indication: Failure to improve after 48-72 hours of antibiotics; suspected abscess; diabetic with severe pyelonephritis (EPN); suspected obstruction not fully evaluated by ultrasound; planned drainage procedure
diagnostic_tests.radiation: Significant radiation dose (especially in young women) — prefer ultrasound when sufficient; avoid unnecessary repeat CT; use CT judiciously

diagnostic_tests.description: A nuclear medicine scan using 99mTc-DMSA which is taken up by functioning renal tubular cells. Acute pyelonephritis shows photon-deficient 'cold' areas (areas of tubular dysfunction from inflammation). Performed 4-6 months after acute infection to detect permanent renal cortical scarring — the most sensitive available method for detecting cortical scars from pyelonephritis. Particularly important in children after febrile UTI to assess for scarring and need for long-term management.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect acute pyelonephritis (early DMSA); detect chronic renal scarring (late DMSA — 4-6 months post-infection); assess renal function distribution (split function)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Cold area on DMSA at 4-6 months post-infection = permanent cortical scar; split function asymmetry >10% = significant relative renal impairment; used to guide investigation and treatment of recurrent childhood UTI (VUR workup)
diagnostic_tests.indication: Children with febrile UTI — particularly first episode in boys and recurrent in girls; assess for scarring and VUR; rarely used in adults

diagnostic_tests.description: A fluoroscopic contrast study of the bladder and urethra during voiding that detects vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) — the retrograde flow of urine from bladder to ureter and kidney. VUR predisposes to ascending pyelonephritis and renal scarring in children. MCUG is the gold standard for VUR detection and grading (I-V).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect vesicoureteric reflux in children after febrile UTI; grade severity of VUR (guides surgical vs conservative management); detect posterior urethral valves (boys)
diagnostic_tests.indication: All male children after first UTI; female children after recurrent febrile UTI or abnormal ultrasound; children with known renal scarring on DMSA
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: VUR Grade I-II: low grade (reflux into ureter only — conservative management); Grade III-IV: moderate (reflux to kidney — may require antibiotic prophylaxis or surgery); Grade V: massive reflux with gross ureteral dilatation — surgical correction

diagnostic_tests.test_name: STI Screen (NAAT for Chlamydia and Gonorrhoea)
diagnostic_tests.description: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) that mimics cystitis and lower UTI in sexually active women. A first-void urine or genital swab NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) for Chlamydia and Gonorrhoea should be considered in sexually active young women presenting with LUTS and pelvic discomfort, particularly if standard urine culture is negative.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose STI mimicking or coexisting with UTI in sexually active young women and men
diagnostic_tests.indication: Sexually active young women with LUTS and negative standard urine culture; urethral discharge; cervicitis; partner with STI

medicines.note: Antibiotic selection for pyelonephritis must be guided by local resistance data and individual patient factors. In India and many parts of South Asia, ESBL-producing E. coli accounts for 30-50% of community UTI isolates — this DRAMATICALLY limits the usefulness of standard oral antibiotics (cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones) for empirical treatment. ALWAYS send urine culture before antibiotics. Start empirical antibiotics based on clinical severity and local resistance patterns, then de-escalate to a targeted narrower-spectrum antibiotic when sensitivity results are available. Adequate oral hydration is a key adjunct to all antibiotic therapy.
treatment_principles: 1. Send MSU for culture and sensitivity BEFORE starting antibiotics — if initiation of antibiotics cannot wait (severe sepsis), send cultures simultaneously within minutes then start antibiotics

2. Choice of antibiotic must be guided by local resistance data — ESBL prevalence is very high in India and community E. coli resistance to fluoroquinolones exceeds 40-60% in many Indian centres; do NOT empirically use fluoroquinolones in areas with high resistance
3. Uncomplicated pyelonephritis in healthy non-pregnant women: oral antibiotics if tolerating fluids; 7-10 days for fluoroquinolones; 14 days for beta-lactams
4. Complicated pyelonephritis, pregnancy, sepsis, vomiting, failure of oral therapy: IV antibiotics in hospital; step-down to oral when afebrile for 24-48 hours and tolerating orally
5. Pyonephrosis or obstruction with infection: DRAINAGE is the primary treatment — antibiotics alone will fail; urgent urology referral for ureteric stenting or nephrostomy
6. NEVER use nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis — achieves inadequate tissue concentrations in kidney; only effective for lower UTI (cystitis)
7. NEVER use nitrofurantoin in pregnancy at term or in renal impairment
8. Adjust antibiotic dose for renal impairment — especially aminoglycosides (nephrotoxic) and renally-cleared antibiotics
9. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin): highly effective but requires therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) for levels and nephrotoxicity
10. De-escalate to narrowest effective antibiotic based on culture results — antibiotic stewardship to reduce resistance

categories.purpose: First-line outpatient management of uncomplicated acute pyelonephritis in non-pregnant adults able to tolerate oral medication.
categories.notes_on_resistance: CRITICAL: Local resistance patterns must guide empirical choice. In India, community E. coli resistance to ciprofloxacin is 40-60% in many regions; co-trimoxazole resistance is 50-70%. This makes many standard first-line regimens unreliable without culture guidance. Urine culture result is essential to guide targeted treatment.

medicines.name: Ciprofloxacin
medicines.dosage: 500 mg twice daily for 7 days (uncomplicated pyelonephritis); 500 mg twice daily for 10-14 days (complicated)
medicines.use_case: First-line oral treatment for uncomplicated pyelonephritis WHERE susceptibility is confirmed on culture or local resistance rates are low (<20%); also covers Staphylococcus saprophyticus; good tissue penetration into renal parenchyma and urine
medicines.mechanism: Fluoroquinolone — inhibits DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV; bactericidal; excellent bioavailability (oral absorption ~80% — nearly equivalent to IV)
medicines.resistance_warning: E. coli resistance to ciprofloxacin has increased dramatically in India (40-70% of community isolates in many centres); do NOT use empirically without culture sensitivity confirmation in high-resistance settings; ESBL-producing organisms are inherently resistant
contraindications: Pregnancy — avoid (animal teratogenicity studies; safer alternatives available)
QT prolongation or use with QT-prolonging drugs
side_effects: Tendinopathy and tendon rupture (Achilles — risk in elderly, steroid users)
medicines.interactions: Avoid with antacids (reduced absorption — separate by 2 hours); dairy products reduce absorption; avoid with warfarin (increases INR)

medicines.name: Levofloxacin
medicines.dosage: 750 mg once daily for 5 days (pyelonephritis); alternatively 500 mg once daily for 7-10 days
medicines.use_case: Alternative fluoroquinolone for uncomplicated pyelonephritis; once-daily dosing improves adherence; slightly broader spectrum than ciprofloxacin (better Gram-positive coverage including Enterococcus); used when culture sensitivity confirmed
medicines.mechanism: Fluoroquinolone — inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; bactericidal; excellent oral bioavailability
medicines.resistance_warning: Cross-resistance with ciprofloxacin — E. coli resistant to ciprofloxacin is almost always resistant to levofloxacin
medicines.contraindications: Same as ciprofloxacin; pregnancy; children under 18

medicines.name: Co-Amoxiclav (Amoxicillin-Clavulanate)
medicines.dosage: 625 mg (500 mg amoxicillin + 125 mg clavulanate) three times daily for 14 days
medicines.use_case: Oral treatment of pyelonephritis caused by susceptible organisms; particularly useful when fluoroquinolone resistance is suspected; active against E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus; safe in pregnancy (most appropriate oral option for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in pregnancy); active against Staph saprophyticus
medicines.mechanism: Beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combination; clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamase enzymes produced by resistant organisms, restoring amoxicillin activity; bactericidal
medicines.resistance_note: ESBL-producing organisms (which produce extended-spectrum beta-lactamases) are resistant to co-amoxiclav — this is increasingly common in India
side_effects: Rash (especially mononucleosis — avoid if glandular fever suspected)

medicines.name: Co-Trimoxazole (Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole / TMP-SMX)
medicines.form: Tablet (480 mg = 400 mg sulphamethoxazole + 80 mg trimethoprim; 960 mg double-strength)
medicines.dosage: 960 mg (double-strength) twice daily for 14 days
medicines.use_case: Oral treatment of pyelonephritis if organism confirmed susceptible on culture; inexpensive; effective; but high resistance rates limit empirical use in India
medicines.mechanism: Synergistic dual blockade of folate synthesis — trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; sulphamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; bactericidal
medicines.resistance_warning: E. coli resistance to co-trimoxazole is 50-70% in India and many developing countries — NOT suitable for empirical treatment; use only when susceptibility confirmed
contraindications: Pregnancy — first trimester (trimethoprim is folate antagonist — risk of neural tube defects); third trimester (risk of neonatal kernicterus)

medicines.name: Cefalexin (Cephalexin)
medicines.dosage: 500 mg four times daily for 14 days
medicines.use_case: Oral first-generation cephalosporin; useful for uncomplicated pyelonephritis with susceptible organisms; safe in pregnancy (preferred oral option in pregnancy when IV ceftriaxone step-down is appropriate); limited spectrum — predominantly Gram-positive and some Gram-negatives
medicines.mechanism: First-generation cephalosporin — beta-lactam; inhibits cell wall synthesis; bactericidal
medicines.limitation: Inferior coverage compared to ciprofloxacin for uncomplicated pyelonephritis; limited Gram-negative spectrum; ESBL-resistant organisms are resistant; requires four times daily dosing (adherence challenge)

medicines.name: Fosfomycin Trometamol
medicines.dosage: 3g single dose dissolved in water (for cystitis); NOT recommended as single dose for pyelonephritis — longer courses needed if used (3g every 48-72 hours for 3-7 days, unlicensed for pyelonephritis)
medicines.use_case: Excellent for uncomplicated cystitis including ESBL-producing E. coli; role in pyelonephritis is EMERGING — some guidelines suggest extended courses for ESBL pyelonephritis in non-severe cases when IV not possible; achieves very high urine concentrations but variable kidney tissue concentrations
medicines.note: NOT first-line for pyelonephritis — standard use is for cystitis; being investigated as oral ESBL alternative; excellent safety profile in pregnancy

categories.category_name: IV Antibiotics — Hospitalised and Complicated Pyelonephritis
categories.purpose: Treatment of complicated, severe, or septic pyelonephritis requiring hospitalisation; initial therapy when oral route is unavailable (vomiting); empirical broad-spectrum cover; targeted treatment of resistant organisms including ESBL.

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone (IV/IM)
medicines.dosage: 1-2 g IV/IM once daily; 2 g IV once daily for severe sepsis
medicines.use_case: First-line IV treatment for moderate to severe community-acquired pyelonephritis with susceptible organisms; third-generation cephalosporin with excellent Gram-negative coverage; step-down to oral when afebrile and tolerating; safe in pregnancy (preferred IV option in pregnancy); also used empirically while awaiting culture results in hospitalised patients
medicines.mechanism: Third-generation cephalosporin — inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins; bactericidal; long half-life (8 hours) allows once-daily dosing; excellent tissue penetration
medicines.limitation: Does NOT cover ESBL-producing organisms — the beta-lactamase produced by ESBL strains hydrolyses cephalosporins including ceftriaxone; does NOT cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa; Enterococcus is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins
medicines.resistance_note: ESBL prevalence is very high in India (30-50%) — where ESBL suspected (prior hospitalisation, prior antibiotics, healthcare exposure, community prevalence), use carbapenem empirically rather than ceftriaxone

medicines.name: Gentamicin (IV/IM) — Aminoglycoside
medicines.dosage: Extended interval dosing: 5 mg/kg IV once daily (in normal renal function); adjust dose and interval in renal impairment based on drug levels; ALWAYS check renal function before prescribing; TDM (therapeutic drug monitoring) required
medicines.use_case: Highly effective for severe pyelonephritis and urosepsis; excellent Gram-negative cover including most ESBL strains; synergistic with beta-lactams; used in combination (gentamicin + amoxicillin or gentamicin + ceftriaxone) for sepsis; BNF/NICE recommended first-line for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in hospital (UK guidance); used in pregnancy for pyelonephritis (risk-benefit favouring treatment); particularly useful when ESBL suspected (retained activity against most ESBL E. coli when given at correct doses)
medicines.mechanism: Aminoglycoside — binds 30S ribosomal subunit; induces misreading of mRNA; bactericidal; concentration-dependent killing (higher peak concentration = better kill)
medicines.monitoring: MANDATORY: pre-dose (trough) level before second dose for extended interval dosing; serum creatinine daily; document baseline renal function; stop if creatinine rising; hearing assessment for prolonged courses (>5 days)
side_effects: NEPHROTOXICITY — dose-dependent; risk increases with dehydration, concurrent NSAIDs, pre-existing renal impairment
OTOTOXICITY — cochlear (high-frequency hearing loss) and vestibular (balance disturbance) — irreversible; risk with prolonged courses
contraindications: Avoid in severe pre-existing renal failure without dose adjustment
Caution in pregnancy — risk of ototoxicity to fetus (8th nerve damage); use when benefit clearly outweighs risk

medicines.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo / Tazocin)
medicines.dosage: 4.5 g (4 g piperacillin + 0.5 g tazobactam) IV every 6-8 hours; 4.5 g every 6 hours for severe sepsis or Pseudomonas risk
medicines.use_case: Broad-spectrum empirical treatment of complicated pyelonephritis and urosepsis when Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a risk (hospital-acquired, catheter-associated, structural urological disease, prior Pseudomonas infection); also covers Enterococcus faecalis; extended spectrum vs piperacillin alone due to tazobactam beta-lactamase inhibitor; NOT reliable for ESBL-producing organisms (tazobactam does not reliably inhibit ESBL enzymes — use carbapenems for ESBL)
medicines.mechanism: Broad-spectrum penicillin/beta-lactamase inhibitor combination; piperacillin has antipseudomonal activity; tazobactam inhibits many beta-lactamases
medicines.resistance_note: NOT reliable for ESBL — despite containing a beta-lactamase inhibitor, piperacillin-tazobactam is not recommended for definitive treatment of ESBL pyelonephritis in current guidelines (MERINO trial showed inferior outcomes vs meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia)
side_effects: Neurotoxicity at high doses in renal impairment (encephalopathy, myoclonus)

medicines.name: Ertapenem (IV/IM)
medicines.dosage: 1 g IV/IM once daily
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE IV TREATMENT FOR ESBL-PRODUCING PYELONEPHRITIS — ertapenem is the preferred carbapenem for community and hospital ESBL pyelonephritis; once-daily dosing; does NOT cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa (advantage — spares broader carbapenems for resistant Pseudomonas); excellent for step-down following initial meropenem in stable ESBL pyelonephritis patients
medicines.mechanism: Group 1 carbapenem — ultra-broad spectrum beta-lactam; resistant to ESBL and most carbapenemases except metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM); inhibits cell wall synthesis
medicines.note: Preferred carbapenem for ESBL pyelonephritis — preserves meropenem/imipenem for carbapenem-resistant organisms (antimicrobial stewardship)

medicines.name: Meropenem (IV)
medicines.dosage: 0.5-1 g IV every 8 hours; 1-2 g every 8 hours for severe sepsis, Pseudomonas, or carbapenem-resistant organisms
medicines.use_case: Treatment of severe urosepsis; ESBL-producing pyelonephritis; hospital-acquired MDR Gram-negative pyelonephritis with Pseudomonas; carbapenem-resistant organisms (combined with other agents); empirical treatment in ICU patients with severe sepsis from urinary source in high-resistance settings
medicines.mechanism: Group 2 carbapenem — broadest spectrum commercially available antibiotic; covers ESBL, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter (variable), Enterococcus faecalis
medicines.stewardship_note: Reserve for confirmed ESBL or Pseudomonas; do not use routinely for uncomplicated community pyelonephritis — inappropriate use drives carbapenem resistance; use ertapenem preferentially for ESBL where Pseudomonas not a concern
side_effects: Seizures at high doses in renal impairment
Broad-spectrum disruption of gut microbiome — C. difficile risk

medicines.name: Amoxicillin IV (or Ampicillin IV) — for Enterococcus
medicines.dosage: Amoxicillin 1 g IV every 8 hours; Ampicillin 1-2 g IV every 6 hours
medicines.use_case: Treatment of Enterococcus faecalis pyelonephritis (confirmed on culture); often combined with gentamicin (synergistic for enterococcal endocarditis and bacteraemia); important gap — cephalosporins do NOT cover Enterococcus; also used for Group B Streptococcus pyelonephritis in pregnancy
medicines.note: Not used empirically for pyelonephritis (inadequate Gram-negative coverage alone) — add gentamicin or ceftriaxone for empirical cover in sepsis until culture confirms Enterococcus

medicines.name: Vancomycin (IV) — for Resistant Gram-Positive Organisms
medicines.dosage: 15-20 mg/kg IV every 8-12 hours (weight-based); AUC-guided dosing preferred; TDM essential
medicines.use_case: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) renal abscess or pyelonephritis; Enterococcus resistant to amoxicillin (non-VRE); penicillin-allergic patients with Gram-positive pyelonephritis; catheter-related Staphylococcal infection
medicines.mechanism: Glycopeptide — inhibits late-stage cell wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala peptidoglycan precursors; bactericidal for Staph; bacteriostatic for Enterococcus
medicines.monitoring: AUC/MIC ratio monitoring for efficacy and toxicity; renal function daily — nephrotoxic; audiology if prolonged
side_effects: Red man syndrome (histamine-mediated — from rapid infusion; prevent by slow infusion)

medicines.name: Fluconazole (IV and Oral) — Fungal Pyelonephritis
medicines.dosage: 200-400 mg IV or oral once daily for 14 days (Candida pyelonephritis); 200 mg once daily for Candida cystitis (7-14 days)
medicines.use_case: Candida urinary tract infection including ascending pyelonephritis in diabetics, catheterised patients, immunocompromised, and post-antibiotics; check Candida species before fluconazole — C. glabrata and C. krusei inherently resistant
medicines.mechanism: Azole antifungal — inhibits ergosterol synthesis by inhibiting lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase; fungistatic against most Candida
medicines.note: Remove urinary catheter if possible (reduces fungal load); correct predisposing factors (hyperglycaemia, discontinue unnecessary antibiotics); urological drainage if fungal ball obstructing collecting system

categories.category_name: Analgesia, Antipyretics, and Antiemetics — Symptomatic Treatment
categories.purpose: Manage pain, fever, nausea, and vomiting while antibiotic therapy addresses the underlying infection.

medicines.name: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 500-1000 mg every 4-6 hours (max 4g/day); Children: 10-15 mg/kg every 4-6 hours
medicines.use_case: First-line antipyretic (fever reduction) and analgesic for loin pain and headache in pyelonephritis; safe in pregnancy (first-line analgesic and antipyretic); safe in mild-moderate renal impairment (preferred over NSAIDs)
medicines.note: IV paracetamol (1g every 6 hours) for hospital use when oral route not available

medicines.name: Ibuprofen / NSAIDs
medicines.dosage: 400-600 mg every 6-8 hours with food and adequate hydration
medicines.use_case: Pain and fever in pyelonephritis when adequately hydrated and no renal impairment; particularly useful for renal colic-type pain from ureteric stone with associated pyelonephritis
contraindications_in_pyelonephritis: Dehydration — NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion via prostaglandin inhibition; precipitates AKI
Known or suspected AKI (rising creatinine) — ABSOLUTELY contraindicated
Pregnancy (all trimesters — fetal renal toxicity; premature ductus arteriosus closure in third trimester)
Urosepsis — avoid (impairs renal autoregulation in sepsis-induced vasodilatation)

medicines.name: Ondansetron
medicines.dosage: 4-8 mg orally, IV, or IM every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: First-line antiemetic for nausea and vomiting in pyelonephritis — allows oral hydration and oral antibiotic administration; IV ondansetron in hospital when vomiting prevents oral route; ODT (oral dissolving tablet) can be placed under the tongue in vomiting patients
medicines.note: Single dose of IV ondansetron in emergency department may allow discharge with oral antibiotics (avoiding admission) if vomiting resolves and patient able to hydrate orally

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dosage: 10 mg oral or IV every 8 hours (max 5 days)
