medicines.use_case: Antiemetic and prokinetic for nausea and vomiting; alternative to ondansetron; useful when IV route required; also facilitates gastric emptying
medicines.side_effects: Extrapyramidal reactions (especially young women and children); avoid in children under 18 — use ondansetron instead

medicines.name: Tramadol / Morphine (Opioids for Severe Pain)
medicines.dosage: Tramadol: 50-100 mg oral every 4-6 hours; Morphine: 2.5-10 mg IV/IM every 4 hours (dose titrated to pain)
medicines.use_case: Severe loin pain not adequately controlled by paracetamol/NSAIDs; obstructing ureteric stone with severe renal colic; post-nephrostomy/procedure pain
medicines.note: Use at lowest effective dose; opioid sedation may mask clinical deterioration — reassess frequently; avoid in patients with haemodynamic instability (vasodilatory effect); consider opioid prescription guidance for discharge

categories.category_name: IV Fluid Resuscitation and Oral Rehydration
categories.purpose: Correct dehydration from fever, vomiting, and reduced oral intake; maintain adequate urine output (essential for antibiotic excretion and renal perfusion); restore haemodynamic stability in sepsis.

medicines.name: Oral Rehydration and Adequate Fluid Intake
medicines.dosage: Minimum 2-3 litres of fluids daily during treatment and recovery; more if fever and sweating
medicines.use_case: All pyelonephritis patients — even those on IV antibiotics should be encouraged to take oral fluids as soon as vomiting resolves; adequate urinary flow helps flush bacteria from urinary tract
medicines.recommended_fluids: Water (primary); ORS sachets if significantly dehydrated from vomiting; coconut water (natural electrolytes); dilute squash or juice; avoid caffeinated beverages (bladder irritant)

medicines.name: Ringer's Lactate (Hartmann's Solution) / Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl)
medicines.dosage: Mild-moderate dehydration: 500 mL-1L IV over 1-2 hours, then reassess; Sepsis resuscitation: 500 mL crystalloid IV bolus over 15-30 minutes, repeat if haemodynamically unstable (total 30 mL/kg); Maintenance: 1-2 mL/kg/hour after resuscitation; monitor urine output (target >0.5 mL/kg/hour)
medicines.use_case: All hospitalised pyelonephritis patients with dehydration, vomiting, or haemodynamic compromise; sepsis resuscitation
medicines.note: Ringer's Lactate (Hartmann's) preferred over large volumes of 0.9% normal saline (normal saline causes hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis in large volumes); reassess frequently — avoid fluid overload in AKI or elderly patients (risk of pulmonary oedema)

categories.category_name: Long-Term Prophylactic Antibiotics (for Recurrent UTI/Pyelonephritis Prevention)
categories.purpose: Reduce frequency of recurrent UTI and pyelonephritis in women with >2 documented UTIs in 6 months or >3 in 12 months, or recurrence causing significant morbidity.

medicines.name: Trimethoprim (Low-Dose Prophylaxis)
medicines.dosage: 100 mg at night (before bed) for 3-6 months; OR post-coital single dose 100-200 mg for sexual intercourse-triggered UTI
medicines.use_case: Recurrent UTI prophylaxis in women (>2 UTIs in 6 months); post-coital prophylaxis; reduces UTI frequency by 95% while on prophylaxis; monitor for resistance on breakthrough infections
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase — static suppression of bacterial growth in urinary tract at night when urinary stasis is greatest

medicines.name: Nitrofurantoin (Low-Dose Prophylaxis)
medicines.dosage: 50-100 mg at night for prophylaxis (3-6 months); OR post-coital single dose 50-100 mg
medicines.use_case: Recurrent UTI prophylaxis in women; post-coital prophylaxis; good resistance profile for E. coli UTI prophylaxis; safe during second trimester of pregnancy for prophylaxis
medicines.CRITICAL_note: NEVER USE FOR PYELONEPHRITIS TREATMENT — nitrofurantoin achieves high urine concentrations but inadequate renal tissue and blood concentrations; effective ONLY for lower UTI (cystitis); use for prophylaxis only, not acute treatment
side_effects: Pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis — rare; associated with prolonged use)

medicines.name: Cefalexin (Low-Dose Prophylaxis)
medicines.dosage: 125-250 mg at night for prophylaxis
medicines.use_case: Recurrent UTI prophylaxis in pregnancy; post-coital prophylaxis; safe in all trimesters of pregnancy; alternative when trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin contraindicated

medicines.name: Vaginal Oestrogen Cream/Pessary (Post-Menopausal Women)
medicines.dosage: Apply intravaginally 2-3 times per week (after initial daily loading for 2 weeks)
medicines.use_case: Post-menopausal women with recurrent UTI from oestrogen-deficiency-related atrophy of vaginal and periurethral mucosa; oestrogen restores Lactobacillus flora and normalises periurethral flora reducing E. coli colonisation; highly effective and safer than prolonged antibiotics in this group
medicines.mechanism: Local oestrogen restores glycogen-rich vaginal epithelium; supports Lactobacillus growth which produces lactic acid (low pH inhibits E. coli periurethral colonisation); restores protective mucous layer of urethra
medicines.note: Minimal systemic absorption with local application; safe in most women; discuss individual suitability with GP or gynaecologist; NOT recommended if history of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer without specialist advice

categories.purpose: Non-antibiotic approaches to reducing UTI recurrence and supporting urinary health.

medicines.name: D-Mannose
medicines.dosage: 2 g daily in water (prevention); 2 g every 2-3 hours for 3 days (acute episode — adjunct only)
medicines.use_case: Prevention of recurrent UTI from E. coli — D-mannose competitively binds type 1 fimbriae (P-pili) of E. coli preventing adhesion to uroepithelium; excreted in urine after oral ingestion. RCT evidence: D-mannose 2g daily significantly reduces UTI recurrence (comparable to nitrofurantoin prophylaxis in some studies). Safe, non-antibiotic approach; minimal side effects
medicines.mechanism: Competitive inhibition of E. coli uroepithelial adhesion — D-mannose saturates E. coli type 1 fimbriae receptors, preventing bacterial attachment to bladder urothelium; bacteria are washed out with urination
side_effects: Mild GI upset (loose stools at high doses)
Safe in pregnancy — no evidence of harm
medicines.evidence: Kranjcec et al. RCT (World J Urol 2014): D-mannose 2g daily significantly reduced recurrence in women with recurrent UTI (recurrence rate 14.6% vs 60.8% placebo and comparable to nitrofurantoin 50mg nightly)

medicines.name: Cranberry Preparations (Cranberry Extract / Juice)
medicines.dosage: Cranberry extract: 200-400 mg twice daily; or 300-400 mL unsweetened cranberry juice daily
medicines.use_case: Prevention of recurrent UTI in women — proanthocyanidins (PACs) in cranberries inhibit type P fimbriae of E. coli preventing adhesion to urothelium. 2023 Cochrane review: cranberry products reduce UTI recurrence in women, children, and people susceptible to UTI; modest but meaningful benefit. Not treatment for acute pyelonephritis — adjunct prevention only
medicines.mechanism: Proanthocyanidins (PAC type A) specifically inhibit P-fimbriated E. coli adhesion to mannose-resistant receptors on uroepithelium; reduces uroepithelial colonisation
medicines.evidence: Cochrane review 2023 (Jepson et al.): cranberry products reduce risk of symptomatic UTI by approximately 26% vs placebo in women with recurrent UTI
medicines.note: Must be unsweetened to avoid excessive sugar (which promotes E. coli growth); not proven to treat established pyelonephritis — prevention only; limited absorption of PACs from juice compared to concentrated extract

medicines.name: Probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GR-1 and Lactobacillus reuteri RC-14 — Vaginal Probiotics)
medicines.dosage: 1-2 capsules daily containing minimum 1 billion CFU of L. rhamnosus GR-1 + L. reuteri RC-14
medicines.use_case: Prevention of recurrent UTI in pre- and post-menopausal women; restoring vaginal Lactobacillus flora reduces periurethral E. coli colonisation and ascending UTI risk. Evidence supports use for both vaginal health and reduction of UTI recurrence. Must be specific strains (GR-1/RC-14 shown to colonise vagina after oral ingestion)
medicines.mechanism: Specific Lactobacillus strains colonise vaginal and periurethral mucosa after oral ingestion; produce H2O2, lactic acid, and bacteriocins that inhibit E. coli, Klebsiella, and other pathogens from colonising periurethral area

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet in pyelonephritis has two distinct phases: (1) Acute treatment phase — focusing on optimal hydration to support antibiotic efficacy, flush bacteria from the urinary tract, and maintain renal perfusion; and (2) Recovery and prevention phase — dietary strategies to reduce UTI recurrence, support bladder and kidney health, and restore gut microbiome after antibiotic treatment. No specific 'pyelonephritis diet' exists, but evidence-based dietary principles significantly influence outcomes and recurrence risk.

phase_1_acute_treatment.priority: HYDRATION IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT DIETARY INTERVENTION IN ACUTE PYELONEPHRITIS
phase_1_acute_treatment.fluid_target: 2.5-3 litres of fluids per day minimum during antibiotic treatment; increase to 3-3.5L during high fever (additional 500mL per degree of temperature above 37°C)
phase_1_acute_treatment.rationale: Adequate hydration: dilutes bacterial concentration in urine; promotes high urine flow rate — mechanical flushing of bacteria from the urinary tract; maintains renal perfusion during sepsis and NSAID use; promotes antibiotic excretion in urine at adequate bactericidal concentrations; prevents stone formation (particularly important in patients with nephrolithiasis)

recommended_acute_phase.benefit: Most important fluid; dilutes urine reducing bacterial and crystal concentration; take 1-2 glasses with each antibiotic dose to ensure adequate urine concentration
recommended_acute_phase.frequency: 8-10 glasses (200 mL each) daily minimum; more with fever

recommended_acute_phase.benefit: Replaces electrolytes lost from fever, sweating, and vomiting; glucose-sodium co-transport maintains hydration better than plain water; essential if significant vomiting has occurred
recommended_acute_phase.frequency: 1-2 sachets in 1L water per day during acute illness, especially if vomiting has occurred

recommended_acute_phase.benefit: Natural electrolyte balance (potassium, sodium, magnesium); near-isotonic; well-tolerated when nauseous; gentle on stomach; provides natural sugars for energy; excellent hydration fluid during acute illness

recommended_acute_phase.food_or_drink: Clear soups and broths (chicken or vegetable)
recommended_acute_phase.benefit: Hydration plus electrolytes and amino acids; sodium encourages water retention; easily digested when nauseous and anorexic; warm soothing effect; protein for immune function
Anti-nausea properties (blocks 5-HT3 vomiting reflex — same mechanism as ondansetron); anti-inflammatory gingerols; warm fluid contributing to hydration; gentle on inflamed mucosa

recommended_acute_phase.food_or_drink: Plain white rice, khichdi, toast, banana — BRAT-like diet
recommended_acute_phase.benefit: Easily digestible during acute febrile illness; low fibre — gentle on gut with reduced motility from illness; provides carbohydrate energy; banana provides potassium (lost in vomiting)
recommended_acute_phase.frequency: Small portions every 3-4 hours; advance as appetite improves

items.benefit: 96% water content — excellent supplemental hydration; contains cucurbitacins with mild diuretic effect; potassium; Vitamin C; gentle alkalinising effect on urine; cooling in summer
items.frequency: Daily as snack or in salad

items.benefit: 92% water; lycopene (antioxidant — anti-inflammatory); citrulline (vasodilatory — improves renal blood flow); potassium and Vitamin C; natural diuretic; excellent summer fruit for urinary health
items.frequency: Daily during acute phase and recovery

items.benefit: High water content; alkalinising minerals (potassium, magnesium); celery contains apigenin (mild diuretic compound); spinach provides iron (anaemia from CKD or recurrent infection)

recommended_foods_for_urinary_health.rationale: Pyelonephritis involves significant kidney inflammation from both direct bacterial toxicity and immune-mediated damage; anti-inflammatory diet supports faster resolution and protects kidney tissue

items.benefit: Curcumin — the most extensively studied natural anti-inflammatory compound; inhibits NF-κB inflammatory pathway; reduces renal inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1β); nephroprotective in experimental models; anti-bacterial synergistic properties; essential Indian spice with high safety profile. Black pepper (piperine) increases curcumin bioavailability by 2000%.
items.frequency: Daily in cooking; turmeric golden milk (haldi doodh) at bedtime; use with black pepper for maximum benefit

items.benefit: Allicin — potent broad-spectrum antimicrobial including activity against E. coli; inhibits E. coli adhesion to uroepithelium; anti-biofilm properties (reduces catheter-associated infection); immunostimulatory (enhances natural killer cell activity); anti-inflammatory; traditional Indian remedy with strong mechanistic rationale
items.frequency: 2-3 raw or lightly cooked cloves daily; crush and allow to rest 10 minutes before cooking (activates alliinase enzyme to form allicin)

items.food: Cranberry products (unsweetened cranberry juice or extract)
items.benefit: Proanthocyanidins (PAC) — inhibit E. coli fimbriae adhesion to uroepithelium; evidence-based prevention of recurrent UTI (Cochrane 2023 review); antioxidant; acidifies urine (modest effect); concentrate preferable to juice (higher PAC content, less sugar)
items.frequency: 200-400 mL unsweetened cranberry juice daily OR extract capsules for prevention; not for treatment of acute pyelonephritis
items.note: Avoid full-strength sweetened cranberry juice (high sugar promotes bacteria); avoid if on warfarin (may increase INR)

items.benefit: Rich in polyphenols, flavonoids, and Vitamin C; amla is the richest plant source of Vitamin C (powerful antioxidant, immune stimulant); reduces urinary inflammation; supports renal tubular antioxidant defences; antibacterial flavonoids
items.frequency: Daily — amla particularly valuable in Indian context; amla juice, murabba, or raw

items.food: Fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, rohu, hilsa)
items.benefit: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) — potently anti-inflammatory; reduce renal cytokine production; protect kidney cells during infection-induced oxidative stress; high-quality protein for immune function and renal repair

recommended_foods_for_urinary_health.rationale: Antibiotic treatment for pyelonephritis causes significant disruption of gut and vaginal microbiomes — which then allows E. coli and resistant organisms to colonise; restoring Lactobacillus flora reduces recolonisation risk and recurrent UTI

items.food: Plain yogurt / Dahi with live cultures
items.benefit: Lactobacillus acidophilus, L. bulgaricus — restore gut and vaginal flora after antibiotic disruption; competitive exclusion of E. coli from gut (reduces source of ascending pathogens); general immune support; evidence for reducing UTI recurrence in women
items.frequency: Daily — start during antibiotic course (take 2 hours away from antibiotic dose) and continue for 4-6 weeks after completing antibiotics
items.note: Choose plain, unsweetened yogurt with 'live active cultures' stated on label; avoid flavoured yogurts (added sugar)

items.benefit: Natural probiotics from fermentation; Lactobacillus and Leuconostoc species; improve gut barrier function; reduce endotoxin translocation from gut (a source of gram-negative bacteraemia); support immune function
items.frequency: Regular part of diet during and after antibiotic course

items.benefit: Diverse probiotic content (multiple Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains plus yeasts); more potent probiotic effect than yogurt; emerging evidence for reducing UTI recurrence
items.frequency: Daily during and after antibiotic treatment

recommended_foods_for_urinary_health.category: Vitamin C (Urinary Acidification and Immune Function)
recommended_foods_for_urinary_health.explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) has been proposed to acidify urine (inhibiting bacterial growth which prefers alkaline pH) and enhance neutrophil function. Evidence for clinical UTI prevention is modest but mechanistically plausible.

items.food: Amla (Indian gooseberry) — highest Vitamin C food
items.content: 600-900 mg Vitamin C per 100g (10-20 times that of oranges)
items.frequency: 1-2 amla daily; amla juice, murabba, or raw

items.food: Citrus fruits (oranges, lemon, lime), guava, papaya, kiwi
items.content: Guava: 228 mg/100g; Orange: 53 mg/100g; Papaya: 62 mg/100g
items.note: Consume moderate amounts — excessive citrus can irritate bladder in some people

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Bladder Irritants — Caffeine (Coffee, Strong Tea, Energy Drinks)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Caffeine increases bladder detrusor muscle contractility — increases urgency, frequency, and dysuria, worsening lower urinary symptoms; diuretic effect causes concentrated urine (higher bacterial concentration); acidifies urine (irritant to inflamed urothelium)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Reduce or avoid during acute pyelonephritis and while symptomatic; switch to water, herbal tea, or coconut water; resume moderate consumption (1 cup/day) when fully recovered
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.note: Decaffeinated coffee is NOT irritant-free — other acids in coffee are also bladder irritants

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Alcohol is a potent diuretic (inhibits ADH) — worsening dehydration during illness; bladder irritant increasing urgency and frequency; impairs neutrophil and lymphocyte function (impairs ability to fight infection); ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION with metronidazole (disulfiram-like severe reaction) and with nitrofurantoin (enhanced side effects); reduces medication compliance and recovery
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Complete abstinence during antibiotic course; minimum 48 hours after completing most antibiotics; 72 hours after completing metronidazole or tinidazole

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Capsaicin activates TRPV1 receptors in the bladder urothelium — increases urgency, frequency, and dysuria; worsens inflamed urothelial symptoms; may delay recovery from cystitis component
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Avoid heavily spiced food during acute illness and while LUTS symptomatic; resume normal spice levels when symptoms fully resolve

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Carbonic acid irritates the bladder; high sugar content in sodas promotes bacterial growth; the acidity worsens inflamed urothelial symptoms
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Avoid during acute illness; replace with water and non-carbonated drinks

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: High-Oxalate Foods (for Calcium Oxalate Stone Formers — Relevant if Pyelonephritis Triggered by Stone)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Patients with pyelonephritis from an obstructing calcium oxalate stone should moderately limit high-oxalate foods to reduce stone recurrence
high_oxalate_foods: Spinach (very high oxalate — avoid excessive amounts)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.note: Normal portions of these foods are fine for patients without stones; restriction only applies to confirmed calcium oxalate stone formers; increase calcium intake (absorbs dietary oxalate in gut) and ensure high fluid intake (>2.5L daily)

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Perhaps the single most important dietary risk factor for UTI and pyelonephritis — low fluid intake results in concentrated urine with high bacterial density; reduced urine flow decreases mechanical flushing of bacteria; concentrated urine is more cytotoxic to uroepithelium
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Target pale yellow urine at all times; dark yellow or amber urine indicates dehydration — drink immediately; aim for 2.5-3L fluids daily as a permanent lifestyle change for UTI prevention

sample_meal_plan.note: Acute phase meal plan (days 1-3 of antibiotic treatment); advance to normal diet as tolerated from day 3-4
sample_meal_plan.on_waking: Large glass of water (300-400 mL) with antibiotic dose; fresh lemon squeezed in warm water (Vitamin C, gentle diuretic)
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Plain yogurt with banana and a teaspoon of honey; OR plain daliya (broken wheat porridge with minimal sugar); glass of water or coconut water; avoid strong coffee — switch to weak ginger tea
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: 1-2 glasses water or ORS; 1-2 raw amla or amla juice; cucumber slices (hydrating snack)
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Plain khichdi (moong dal and rice — gentle on digestion) with a little ghee; boiled or steamed vegetables (no heavy spice); glass of buttermilk (chaach) — probiotic; 2 glasses of water
sample_meal_plan.afternoon: Coconut water; watermelon or cucumber; plain crackers if appetite poor
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Clear chicken broth or vegetable soup (hydration, sodium, protein); plain boiled rice or roti with dal (minimal spice); steamed fish if tolerated (omega-3, protein); glass of water
sample_meal_plan.bedtime: Warm turmeric milk (haldi doodh) — anti-inflammatory; 1-2 glasses water (adequate overnight hydration — important for night-time urinary flushing)
general_targets: Urine should be pale yellow at all times
Small frequent meals if appetite poor — do not force large meals during acute illness
Start probiotic yogurt from day 1 of antibiotics — take 2 hours apart from antibiotic dose

hydration_and_voiding_habits.overview: Behavioural and voiding habit modifications are among the most evidence-based non-antibiotic strategies for preventing recurrent UTI and pyelonephritis.
measures: Drink minimum 2.5 litres of fluid daily — the single most important behavioural prevention strategy; targets pale yellow urine; high urine flow mechanically flushes bacteria before they can ascend or adhere
Urinate regularly — do not defer voiding when the urge occurs; target voiding every 3-4 hours; prolonged bladder distension increases uroepithelial vulnerability to bacterial invasion

Post-coital voiding (urination within 15-30 minutes of sexual intercourse) — mechanical flushing removes bacteria milked into the urethra during intercourse; highly effective; reduces post-coital UTI risk by ~50%; drink a glass of water before intercourse to facilitate post-coital urination
Complete bladder emptying — ensure full bladder emptying; lean forward on toilet (women) or double void (urinate, wait 30 seconds, urinate again); residual urine is a bacterial growth medium
Bowel regularity — constipation increases periurethral E. coli load; high-fibre diet, adequate hydration, and bowel habits all influence UTI risk
Wipe front-to-back after defaecation — particularly important in women and girls; prevents faecal E. coli contaminating periurethral area
Avoid prolonged use of indwelling urinary catheters — remove as soon as clinically appropriate; each day of catheterisation increases CAUTI risk by 5-10%
Empty bladder before sleep — reduces overnight urinary stasis when urine flow is lowest
Use unperfumed soap for external genital washing — perfumed soaps and feminine hygiene products disrupt normal vaginal Lactobacillus flora which protects against E. coli colonisation
Avoid vaginal douching — disrupts protective vaginal flora; strongly associated with increased UTI and pelvic inflammatory disease risk

Review contraception method if experiencing recurrent UTI — spermicides kill Lactobacillus flora and significantly increase E. coli periurethral colonisation; change to non-spermicidal condoms, oral contraceptive pill (which does not increase UTI risk), or long-acting reversible contraception (coil, implant)
Shower preference over bath — bath water contains bacteria that can ascend the urethra; showers reduce exposure
Wear breathable cotton underwear — synthetic materials retain moisture, creating warm humid environment favouring bacterial growth in periurethral area
Avoid tight-fitting trousers and underwear — reduce genital area ventilation
Shower and urinate after swimming — pool water, particularly heavily used, can contain bacteria

diabetes: Optimal glycaemic control is the single most important intervention in diabetics with pyelonephritis — hyperglycaemia directly impairs neutrophil function (killing, chemotaxis, adherence), promotes bacterial growth (glucose-rich urine), and autonomic neuropathy impairs bladder emptying
Target HbA1c <53 mmol/mol (7%) — tight glycaemic control significantly reduces UTI risk and severity
Check post-void residual urine volume in diabetics with neuropathy — neurogenic bladder is a major predisposing factor for recurrent UTI; intermittent self-catheterisation if significant residual
Annual urine dipstick and culture for asymptomatic bacteriuria — debate exists whether to treat in diabetics but screen and manage as indicated
Avoid SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins — empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) during active UTI — glycosuria from SGLT2 inhibition promotes urinary bacterial growth; hold during acute infection
urinary_stones: Adequate hydration (>2.5-3L daily) is the most important measure to prevent stone recurrence
Metabolic stone evaluation after first stone in patients <60 years or recurrent stones: 24-hour urine for calcium, oxalate, urate, citrate, creatinine, pH, volume

Dietary modification based on stone type: calcium oxalate — moderate dietary oxalate restriction, adequate (not excessive) calcium intake, reduce animal protein; uric acid — reduce dietary purines (red meat, shellfish), alkalinise urine (potassium citrate)

Struvite (infection stones) — require complete surgical stone removal (bacteria embedded in stone cannot be eradicated by antibiotics without stone removal) plus prolonged antibiotics; acetohydroxamic acid (AHA) — urease inhibitor (adjunct for residual struvite)
vesicoureteric_reflux_management_childre: All children after febrile UTI should be evaluated for VUR (MCUG + DMSA scan) per NICE guidelines

Low-grade VUR (grades I-III): conservative management — antibiotic prophylaxis (trimethoprim or cefalexin nightly) until spontaneous resolution (usually by age 5-6 years); annual MCUG to assess resolution; DMSA scan 6 months after each febrile UTI to monitor for new scarring
High-grade VUR (grades IV-V): surgical correction — laparoscopic or open ureteric reimplantation or endoscopic submucosal injection (Deflux) — reduces reflux and prevents further renal scarring
Long-term monitoring: annual blood pressure (hypertension from renal scarring), annual urine for proteinuria; eGFR monitoring

lifestyle_during_acute_illness: Rest — adequate bed rest during febrile phase; avoid work and strenuous activity until afebrile for at least 24-48 hours
Complete the full antibiotic course — symptoms typically improve within 48-72 hours but bacteria may persist; stopping antibiotics early risks relapse, treatment failure, and antibiotic resistance
Temperature monitoring — check temperature twice daily; fever should resolve within 48-72 hours; persistent fever indicates treatment failure requiring reassessment
Monitor urine output — aim for regular pale-yellow urination; no urination for >8 hours is concerning for AKI
Avoid NSAIDs if dehydrated or renal function impaired

Take antibiotic with a full glass of water and remain upright for 30 minutes (oesophageal irritation prevention with some antibiotics); take oral fluoroquinolones separately from dairy products, antacids, and iron
Return to school/work: not before afebrile for 48 hours; food handlers and healthcare workers may require urine culture clearance

post_treatment_follow_up.test_of_cure: Urine culture 5-7 days after completing antibiotics is recommended in: all pregnant women (mandatory); children; men; recurrent UTI; complicated pyelonephritis; resistant organism identified; immunocompromised patients. Not required routinely in uncomplicated pyelonephritis in otherwise healthy women if symptoms fully resolved.
long_term_follow_up: Blood pressure monitoring — pyelonephritis causing renal scarring can lead to renovascular hypertension; check annually if recurrent pyelonephritis or known scarring
Renal function monitoring — annual U&E and eGFR in patients with: recurrent pyelonephritis, single kidney, known renal scarring, diabetes, hypertension, or age >65 years

Referral to urology if: recurrent pyelonephritis despite appropriate management, structural abnormality identified, stone disease, VUR in children, male with pyelonephritis (all men need urological investigation)
Referral to nephrology if: falling eGFR, proteinuria >300 mg/day, eGFR <60 with rising trend, hypertension difficult to control, suspected interstitial nephritis

pyelonephritis_monitoring_plan.note: This monitoring guide helps determine when home management is safe and when urgent or emergency care is required. Anyone with suspected pyelonephritis (fever + loin pain + urinary symptoms) should be assessed by a doctor on the SAME DAY — this is not a 'wait and see' condition.

green_zone.status: Mild — Outpatient Management (with daily telephone review)
green_zone.criteria: Confirmed or strongly suspected uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a healthy, non-pregnant woman; temperature below 38.5°C; able to drink fluids and take oral medications; no vomiting preventing oral intake; no confusion; heart rate below 100; blood pressure normal; no signs of dehydration; no complicating factors; urine dipstick positive; GP or urgent care assessment completed same day
green_zone.action: Oral antibiotics (ciprofloxacin or co-amoxiclav — guided by local resistance); paracetamol for fever; minimum 2.5-3L oral fluids daily; urine culture sent; telephone review at 24-48 hours; return immediately if worsening; GP review at 7 days and on receipt of culture results to confirm correct antibiotic

yellow_zone.criteria: Any of: persistent vomiting preventing oral medication or hydration; temperature above 39°C; heart rate above 100 bpm; signs of dehydration (dry mouth, dizziness, dark urine, reduced urine output); pregnancy; male sex; diabetes; elderly (>65 years); immunocompromised; known renal disease; no improvement after 24-48 hours of oral antibiotics; recurrent pyelonephritis; first episode in a child
yellow_zone.action: Emergency department or hospital admission assessment; blood cultures before antibiotics; urine culture; IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone or gentamicin); IV fluids for dehydration; antiemetics; renal ultrasound; FBC, CRP, U&E, blood glucose; step-down to oral when tolerating and afebrile; discharge planning with oral antibiotics and follow-up

red_zone.status: EMERGENCY — Call Emergency Services (102/112) or Go to Emergency Department IMMEDIATELY
criteria_immediate: Rigors (uncontrollable violent shivering) — bacteraemia; IV antibiotics needed immediately; blood cultures before antibiotics
Confusion, altered consciousness, or difficulty rousing — urosepsis with organ dysfunction — SEPTIC EMERGENCY
Heart rate above 120 bpm with hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg), cold and clammy skin, mottling — SEPTIC SHOCK
Temperature above 40°C or below 36°C (hypothermia — very serious sign of sepsis in the elderly)
Severe loin pain in a known kidney stone patient with fever and rigors — possible pyonephrosis (obstructed infected kidney) — SURGICAL EMERGENCY; requires emergency urological drainage
No urine output for 8+ hours despite drinking fluids — possible AKI with ureteric obstruction
Diabetic patient with severe pyelonephritis who is worsening despite antibiotics — possible emphysematous pyelonephritis (CT scan urgently)
Fever failing to resolve after 72 hours of appropriate IV antibiotics — possible renal abscess or pyonephrosis requiring imaging and drainage
Pregnant woman with pyelonephritis symptoms — any pregnant woman with fever and loin pain must go to hospital immediately (maternal and foetal emergency risk)
Immunocompromised patient (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy) with pyelonephritis — high risk of rapid deterioration; always requires hospitalisation

complications.description: Bacteraemia from the infected kidney, with progressive sepsis — systemic inflammatory response → organ dysfunction → haemodynamic failure. The urinary tract is the most common source of Gram-negative bacteraemia (E. coli, Klebsiella) in adults. Urosepsis is a medical emergency — mortality increases by 7% for every hour of delay in antibiotic administration beyond the first hour.
complications.severity: Life-threatening — mortality 15-30% in septic shock from urinary source
complications.management: Immediate IV antibiotics (within 1 hour of presentation); IV fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg crystalloid if hypotensive); vasopressors (noradrenaline) for persistent hypotension; ICU admission; blood cultures before antibiotics; source control (emergency drainage of obstruction or abscess); serial lactate monitoring; multidisciplinary team — intensive care, urology, microbiology
complications.prevention: Early diagnosis and treatment of pyelonephritis before sepsis develops; prompt relief of urinary obstruction

complications.description: Acute deterioration of renal function — rising serum creatinine and falling eGFR — occurring in 10-20% of hospitalised pyelonephritis patients. Mechanisms: cytokine-mediated intrarenal vasoconstriction reducing glomerular filtration; direct bacterial endotoxin nephrotoxicity; obstruction (post-renal AKI from stone or pus); haemodynamic compromise in sepsis (pre-renal); nephrotoxic antibiotic effects (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs).
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe — may require renal replacement therapy (dialysis) if severe; most cases fully reversible with appropriate management
complications.management: IV fluid resuscitation to restore renal perfusion; relieve obstruction urgently; avoid nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, nephrotoxic antibiotics if not essential; dose-adjust renally cleared antibiotics); monitor creatinine and urine output daily; nephrology consultation if creatinine rising rapidly or not improving; renal replacement therapy (CRRT) if oliguria persists despite volume replacement

complications.description: Localised collection of pus within (intrarenal) or around (perinephric) the kidney — developing when pyelonephritis fails to respond to antibiotics and bacteria are contained by the host immune response. Presents as persistent fever and loin pain despite 5-7 days of appropriate antibiotics. Perinephric abscess can track into adjacent spaces (psoas muscle — psoas abscess; paraspinal; retroperitoneum).
complications.management: CT-guided percutaneous drainage for abscesses >3-4 cm; prolonged IV then oral antibiotics (total 4-6 weeks); surgical drainage if percutaneous fails; correct underlying cause (relieve obstruction, address stone); repeat imaging to confirm resolution

complications.description: Gas-forming necrotising renal infection in diabetics — see TYPE-03 above. Mortality 21-43%. Requires ICU, IV antibiotics, and urgent percutaneous drainage or nephrectomy. CT scan essential for diagnosis.
complications.management: See TYPE-03; ICU; emergency drainage; aggressive diabetes management; broad-spectrum antibiotics

complications.complication: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) from Renal Scarring
complications.description: Recurrent episodes of pyelonephritis cause progressive renal cortical scarring — loss of functional renal tissue and nephrons over years. Particularly important in children with unrecognised vesicoureteric reflux — 10-15% of childhood end-stage renal disease is attributed to reflux nephropathy from recurrent pyelonephritis. In adults, recurrent complicated pyelonephritis gradually reduces renal reserve.
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe (long-term) — progressive but preventable
complications.management: Prevent recurrent infection (antibiotics, correct VUR, remove infected stones); control hypertension with ACE inhibitors/ARBs (renoprotective and antihypertensive); monitor eGFR annually; nephrology referral for CKD stage 3B+ (eGFR <45); renal replacement planning for end-stage disease

complications.complication: Pregnancy Complications (Preterm Labour, IUGR, Maternal Sepsis)
complications.description: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy carries significantly higher risks than in non-pregnant women. The dilated ureters (progesterone-mediated) and compressed ureters (uterine pressure) predispose to ascending infection and urosepsis. Maternal pyelonephritis causes: preterm labour (10-20% of untreated or delayed-treatment cases — bacterial endotoxins stimulate prostaglandin synthesis triggering uterine contractions); intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) from febrile illness and placental blood flow reduction; maternal septicaemia and septic shock; fetal compromise from maternal hypoxia and hypotension.
complications.severity: Severe — obstetric emergency; all pregnant women with pyelonephritis must be admitted to hospital
complications.management: Hospitalisation mandatory in most cases; IV ceftriaxone (safe in pregnancy) or amoxicillin-clavulanate; IV fluids; antipyretics (paracetamol only — NSAIDs contraindicated); fetal monitoring (CTG); obstetric review; urine culture-guided treatment; test of cure culture after completing antibiotics; low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis (cefalexin) for remainder of pregnancy if recurrent infection; screen for and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria at every antenatal visit

complications.description: Ischaemic necrosis of renal papillae (the tips of renal pyramids) — caused by combination of vascular compromise and bacterial toxicity in diabetics, sickle cell disease, or analgesic nephropathy. Sloughed papillary tissue can obstruct the ureter causing acute loin pain, haematuria (often gross), and worsening renal function. The sloughed papilla may be passed in urine.
complications.risk_groups: Diabetic pyelonephritis; sickle cell disease; chronic NSAID use; obstructive uropathy
complications.management: Aggressive pyelonephritis treatment (IV antibiotics, hydration); relieve ureteric obstruction if sloughed papilla causing blockage (ureteric stent); manage underlying diabetes; avoid NSAIDs

complications.description: Failure of empirical antibiotic treatment from resistant organisms — particularly ESBL-producing E. coli, which is extremely prevalent in India. Treatment failure (persistence of fever and symptoms beyond 72 hours of antibiotics) must trigger: urine culture and sensitivity review (if not yet done); change to appropriately sensitive antibiotic; imaging to exclude abscess or obstruction. Repeated courses of antibiotics select for MDR organisms — each course reduces future antibiotic options.
complications.management: Culture-guided antibiotic de-escalation; switch to carbapenem (ertapenem) for ESBL; antibiotic stewardship — use narrowest appropriate spectrum; prevent recurrence to reduce antibiotic burden; report MDR organisms to infection control and public health

complications.description: See TYPE-06 — infected obstructed kidney with pus in the collecting system. Rapidly fatal without emergency drainage. Antibiotics cannot penetrate the obstructed collecting system effectively.
complications.management: Emergency ureteric stent or nephrostomy; IV antibiotics (adjunctive); ICU; identify and treat cause of obstruction

key_points: Pyelonephritis is the most common serious medical complication of pregnancy — affecting 1-2% of pregnant women; all cases require hospitalisation

Physiological changes of pregnancy directly predispose to ascending UTI: progesterone-mediated smooth muscle relaxation causes ureteral dilation and reduced peristalsis; the growing uterus mechanically compresses the right ureter (right-sided pyelonephritis is more common); reduced bladder capacity increases urinary stasis

Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy — 2-7% of pregnant women; if untreated, 30-40% will progress to symptomatic UTI or pyelonephritis; SCREEN ALL PREGNANT WOMEN at booking (first antenatal visit) with urine culture and TREAT positive ASB

Group B Streptococcus (GBS) detected in urine in pregnancy — even if asymptomatic — must be treated (penicillin/amoxicillin); indicates GBS colonisation and requires IV penicillin prophylaxis in labour to prevent neonatal GBS sepsis

Treatment — pregnancy-safe antibiotics ONLY: ceftriaxone IV (first-line for admitted patients), cefalexin oral (step-down), amoxicillin-clavulanate (step-down); AVOID: fluoroquinolones (arthropathy and cartilage effects in animal studies), aminoglycosides (fetal 8th nerve ototoxicity — use only when life-threatening if no alternative), trimethoprim in first trimester (folate antagonism — neural tube defect risk), nitrofurantoin at term (neonatal haemolysis), tetracyclines
Duration: IV antibiotics until afebrile for 24-48 hours, then oral antibiotics to complete 10-14 day course
Test of cure: mandatory urine culture 7-10 days after completing antibiotics, and at each subsequent antenatal visit
Prophylaxis: if two or more UTIs in pregnancy — antibiotic prophylaxis for remainder of pregnancy (cefalexin 125-250 mg nightly) with monthly urine cultures
Fetal monitoring: continuous fetal heart rate monitoring (CTG) during acute pyelonephritis if >24 weeks gestation; watch for uterine contractions
Recurrence in pregnancy: 30-40% recurrence risk — vigilant antenatal monitoring essential

UTI is the most common serious bacterial infection in infants and the second most common cause of fever without source in children under 5 years; suspicion must be high in febrile children without obvious source
All febrile children under 2 years without obvious focus: urine culture is mandatory — pyelonephritis may present with fever alone (no localising urinary symptoms)
Clean-catch midstream urine is ideal — avoid bag specimens in nappies (very high contamination rate of 90% false positives); catheter or suprapubic aspirate for infants unable to produce clean catch
Treatment: cefalexin oral (mild); IV ceftriaxone (moderate-severe); IV gentamicin + amoxicillin (sepsis); step-down to oral after 48-72 hours IV
Duration: 7-14 days total (10 days recommended for febrile UTI in children)

Vesicoureteric reflux investigation: all males after first UTI; females after second UTI or with abnormal ultrasound — renal ultrasound, DMSA scintigraphy 4-6 months post-infection, MCUG for VUR detection
Antibiotic prophylaxis: all children with VUR grades III-V; children with recurrent UTI or single kidney; cefalexin or trimethoprim nightly until VUR resolves
Renal scarring: DMSA scan at 4-6 months after febrile UTI — permanent scars visible; 30-60% of children with VUR develop some scarring after pyelonephritis
Constipation in children dramatically increases UTI risk — always assess and treat constipation in a child with recurrent UTIs
Paediatric urology and paediatric nephrology referral for VUR, renal scarring, or recurrent pyelonephritis

Pyelonephritis in the elderly is frequently atypical — new or worsening confusion (delirium) is the most common presenting feature; fever is often absent or blunted (immunosenescence); falls, reduced mobility, anorexia, and urinary incontinence may be the sole presentation
UTI is the most common cause of acute confusion (delirium) in elderly women — ALWAYS check urinalysis and culture in any acutely confused elderly patient

However, CAUTION: bacteriuria is extremely common in elderly (30-50% of women over 80 have asymptomatic bacteriuria) — a positive urine dipstick in a confused elderly person does NOT automatically mean UTI is the CAUSE of confusion; other causes of delirium (medication, cardiac, respiratory, neurological) must be excluded
Hydration assessment is more challenging in the elderly — reduced thirst sensation; look for postural hypotension, dry mucous membranes, and urine output
Multiple comorbidities in elderly patients (diabetes, CKD, heart failure, BPH) all increase pyelonephritis severity and complications

BPH (benign prostatic hypertrophy) in elderly men causes incomplete bladder emptying — a key risk factor for recurrent UTI and pyelonephritis; urological evaluation for post-void residual urine and BPH treatment essential

Antibiotic selection: check renal function before prescribing (renally excreted antibiotics); reduce gentamicin doses and monitor carefully for nephrotoxicity; avoid nitrofurantoin if eGFR <30; fluoroquinolone tendon rupture risk is higher in elderly — use with caution
Lower threshold for hospital admission; faster decompensation to sepsis; post-discharge functional recovery may take weeks
UTI in men is by definition a 'complicated UTI' — the longer male urethra and prostate secretions make ascending UTI unusual without a predisposing cause
All men with pyelonephritis must be investigated for underlying urological abnormality: BPH, urethral stricture, prostate cancer, urinary stone, structural renal abnormality, recent instrumentation

Prostatitis must be excluded — bacterial prostatitis can cause fever, loin pain, and UTI symptoms; distinguish by: prostate tenderness on rectal examination (gentle examination — vigorous massage risks bacteraemia); PSA elevation (prostatitis significantly raises PSA — do NOT check PSA during active infection); requires 4-6 weeks of antibiotics (fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim — achieves adequate prostatic tissue penetration)
Treatment duration for male pyelonephritis: 10-14 days minimum (vs 7 days uncomplicated female); if prostatitis coexists: 4-6 weeks

Antibiotic choice for male UTI: fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) have excellent prostatic tissue penetration — preferred for male UTI if susceptible organism; trimethoprim also achieves good prostatic penetration
Urology referral: all men after first episode of pyelonephritis or unexplained UTI — renal and bladder ultrasound, post-void residual, urine flow rate; cystoscopy if structural abnormality suspected

HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200), transplant recipients, chemotherapy patients, high-dose steroid users, and biologic therapy patients have dramatically higher risk of severe, unusual, and recurrent pyelonephritis

Fungal pyelonephritis (Candida) is an important diagnosis in immunocompromised, catheterised, and post-antibiotic patients — screen for Candida in urine culture when clinical picture does not respond to antibacterial antibiotics
Consider atypical organisms: Cryptococcus neoformans, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (renal TB), CMV, BK virus (transplant patients)
Transplant recipients: BK virus nephropathy causes nephritis mimicking pyelonephritis; check BK virus PCR in blood and urine in transplant patients with renal dysfunction
Renal TB: haematuria, sterile pyuria (WBCs in urine with negative standard bacterial culture), upper tract scarring — 'morning urine' Mycobacterial culture essential; 6-12 month anti-TB therapy
Lower threshold for IV antibiotics, imaging, and longer antibiotic courses; culture-guided therapy essential
Antibiotic prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole) in HIV/AIDS and transplant recipients also reduces UTI risk but TMP-SMX resistance limits its efficacy for treatment
Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) is the most common healthcare-associated infection; every day of urinary catheterisation increases bacteriuria by 5-10%

CRITICAL PRINCIPLE: Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterised patients — a positive urine culture in a catheterised patient without symptoms (fever, new confusion, loin pain, haemodynamic instability) is colonisation, not infection; treating asymptomatic bacteriuria drives resistance and C. difficile
Treat CAUTI only if: fever >38°C without other source, new confusion, loin pain, haemodynamic instability, or pre-operatively

Catheter should be changed if in situ more than 48-72 hours before sending urine culture for CAUTI investigation — existing catheter is colonised with biofilm bacteria that do not represent true infection; new catheter sample is more representative
Antibiotic choice: guided by culture — Pseudomonas and ESBL are more common in catheter-related infection than community UTI

Prevention: remove urinary catheters as early as clinically possible; strict catheter care (closed drainage system, secure catheter to prevent trauma, regular drainage bag emptying with sterile technique, meatal hygiene); use smallest effective catheter gauge; consider intermittent catheterisation over indwelling where possible (lower infection risk)

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Annually before flu season (October-November in India)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza causes significant immunosuppression, increasing susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections including pyelonephritis. Elderly patients and diabetics with influenza are at particular risk of secondary bacteraemia from urinary sources. All patients with recurrent pyelonephritis — particularly elderly, diabetics, and immunocompromised — should receive annual influenza vaccination.
vaccinations_recommended.effectiveness: 40-60% efficacy (varies with strain match); significantly reduces secondary bacterial infections

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: PCV15 or PCV20 once; PPSV23 booster in high-risk groups
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients hospitalised with urosepsis are at risk of secondary pneumococcal pneumonia and bacteraemia in the post-sepsis immunosuppressed state. Elderly (>65 years) with pyelonephritis and those with renal impairment should be up to date with pneumococcal vaccination.
vaccinations_recommended.indication: All adults >65 years; all patients with CKD from recurrent pyelonephritis

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Primary series and boosters per national schedule
vaccinations_recommended.reason: COVID-19 infection is associated with exacerbation of pre-existing UTI and increased risk of secondary bacterial infections. Diabetics and immunocompromised patients (high-risk groups for pyelonephritis) are at higher risk of severe COVID-19 and secondary bacterial infections. Ensure all vulnerable patients with recurrent pyelonephritis are fully vaccinated against COVID-19.
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Follow national vaccination schedule; particularly important in diabetics and immunocompromised

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Injectable Vi polysaccharide single dose (booster every 3 years); or oral Ty21a 4 capsules (booster every 5 years)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Salmonella Typhi bacteraemia during typhoid fever can seed to the kidneys causing nephritis and pyelonephritis (salmonella pyelonephritis). In India and endemic areas, typhoid fever can be complicated by urinary tract involvement. Typhoid vaccination protects against the primary infection and reduces complication risk.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Particularly relevant for travel to endemic areas and for residents of areas with poor sanitation

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis B can cause membranous nephropathy and glomerulonephritis which increases susceptibility to urinary tract infections. Patients with chronic kidney disease from recurrent pyelonephritis should be vaccinated against hepatitis B (reduced immune response requires higher dose or additional booster doses in CKD).
vaccinations_recommended.note: Patients with eGFR <30 may require double-dose hepatitis B vaccine (40 mcg instead of 20 mcg) due to impaired immune response

when_to_see_doctor: ANY suspected pyelonephritis — fever with loin/flank pain with or without urinary symptoms — requires SAME DAY medical assessment; do not wait for symptoms to progress
Fever above 38°C with any of the following: loin or back pain, burning on urination, frequent urination, nausea and vomiting, or general severe illness
Burning on urination (dysuria) and urinary frequency without fever (cystitis) — same-day GP appointment; urine culture required; do not treat with over-the-counter remedies without medical evaluation
Symptoms not improving within 24-48 hours of starting antibiotics for UTI — possible resistant organism, pyelonephritis not cystitis, or complication developing
Haematuria (blood in urine) — all cases require urine culture and appropriate investigation to exclude bladder cancer (in over 50s), kidney stones, and glomerulonephritis in addition to UTI
Male patient with any UTI symptoms — see doctor same day; all male UTI requires urological investigation
Pregnant woman with any urinary symptoms — urgent same-day assessment; pyelonephritis in pregnancy is a medical emergency
Child under 2 years with fever and no obvious source — urine culture mandatory; do not assume viral illness without testing
Recurrent UTIs (2+ in 6 months or 3+ in 12 months) — GP review to investigate underlying cause, consider prophylaxis, urological referral, and lifestyle interventions
Diabetic with UTI symptoms — same-day medical review; higher risk of severe disease and emphysematous pyelonephritis
Elderly person with new confusion or fall with or without urinary symptoms — always send urine culture as part of delirium workup
History of renal stones with new fever and loin pain — urgent assessment for obstructing infected stone (pyonephrosis risk)
Immunocompromised patient with urinary symptoms or fever — same-day assessment; higher risk of severe disease and unusual organisms
Post-treatment: fever or symptoms returning within 2 weeks of completing antibiotic course — possible relapse or recurrence; send urine culture before restarting antibiotics
emergency_signs: Rigors (uncontrollable violent shivering with extreme chills lasting 15-30 minutes) followed by high fever and sweating — BACTERAEMIA — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112/999/911) and go to emergency department; blood cultures and IV antibiotics needed immediately
Confusion, altered consciousness, or inability to rouse — UROSEPSIS with organ dysfunction — EMERGENCY; call emergency services
Heart rate above 120 bpm with hypotension (systolic BP below 90 mmHg), cold clammy skin, mottling — SEPTIC SHOCK — life-threatening emergency; call emergency services immediately
Temperature above 40°C or below 36°C (hypothermia — particularly ominous in elderly) — SEVERE SEPSIS — EMERGENCY
No urine output for 8+ hours despite adequate fluid intake with high fever and loin pain — possible obstructing infected stone with AKI — EMERGENCY; urology and nephrology needed urgently

Severe loin pain radiating to groin with high fever and vomiting — possible pyonephrosis (obstructed infected kidney) — SURGICAL EMERGENCY; requires emergency ureteric drainage; antibiotics alone will fail
Pregnant woman with fever above 38°C and loin pain — obstetric emergency; risk of preterm labour and maternal sepsis — go to hospital maternity unit immediately

Diabetic patient with worsening fever despite 48-72 hours of antibiotics — possible emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in kidney); CT scan urgently needed; emergency surgical or drainage intervention may be required
Palpable tender flank mass in febrile patient — possible large renal or perinephric abscess requiring emergency drainage
Fever persisting beyond 72 hours of appropriate IV antibiotics — failure to respond; urgent CT scan for abscess or obstruction; change antibiotics pending culture results
Child with high fever, loin tenderness, and very reduced urine output — possible AKI from pyelonephritis; paediatric emergency

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between a kidney infection (pyelonephritis) and a bladder infection (cystitis)?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Both are urinary tract infections (UTIs) but they affect different parts of the urinary tract and have different severity. Cystitis (lower UTI) affects only the bladder — causing burning on urination, urinary frequency, urgency, and sometimes blood in the urine, but NOT fever or loin pain. It is uncomfortable but not dangerous for most people. Pyelonephritis (upper UTI / kidney infection) occurs when bacteria ascend from the bladder to infect the kidney itself — causing high fever (often with rigors/shivering), flank/loin pain, and systemic illness (nausea, vomiting, weakness) in addition to urinary symptoms. Pyelonephritis is significantly more serious — it can cause bacteraemia (bacteria in the blood), septic shock, and permanent kidney damage if untreated. Fever with loin pain = pyelonephritis until proven otherwise — requires same-day medical assessment.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What causes pyelonephritis and why do women get it more than men?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Pyelonephritis is almost always caused by bacteria (most commonly Escherichia coli — the bacterium normally found in the bowel) ascending from the lower urinary tract to the kidneys. Women get pyelonephritis far more commonly (7-10 times) than men for anatomical reasons: the female urethra is only 3-4 cm long compared to 20 cm in men, making it much easier for bacteria from the periurethral area (near the vagina and anus) to travel to the bladder and then up to the kidneys. Sexual activity, pregnancy, and menopause (oestrogen deficiency reducing protective vaginal flora) are major additional risk factors. In men, the longer urethra and prostate secretions with antibacterial properties protect against ascending infection — any UTI in a man is considered unusual and should prompt investigation for an underlying cause.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How is pyelonephritis treated and do I need to be admitted to hospital?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Most uncomplicated cases in healthy young women can be treated with oral antibiotics at home — provided nausea and vomiting are not preventing fluid and medication intake and fever is not extremely high. However, hospital admission is needed for: pregnant women (all cases), men (always investigated as complicated), elderly patients (faster dehydration and delirium risk), diabetics (risk of severe emphysematous pyelonephritis), anyone with significant vomiting, signs of sepsis, or no improvement within 24-48 hours of oral antibiotics. In hospital, IV antibiotics are given until fever resolves (usually 24-48 hours), then switched to oral to complete the course. CRITICAL in India and high-ESBL-prevalence areas: always send urine culture before antibiotics — E. coli resistant to standard oral antibiotics (ESBL-producing strains) is extremely common, and blind empirical treatment may fail without culture guidance.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why is there so much antibiotic resistance in UTI and pyelonephritis now?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Antibiotic resistance in urinary tract infections — particularly from ESBL-producing E. coli — has become a critical problem globally, and especially in India. ESBL (extended-spectrum beta-lactamase) is an enzyme that many E. coli strains now carry that destroys most common antibiotics (cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, and often fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin). In some Indian cities, 40-60% of community E. coli UTI isolates now produce ESBL — meaning standard oral antibiotics do not work for nearly half of patients. Causes include: overuse and misuse of antibiotics (self-medication without prescription, not completing courses), use of antibiotics in animal farming (shared resistance genes), spread through contaminated water and food, and international travel. This is why urine culture before antibiotics is so important — without knowing the organism's sensitivity profile, choosing the right antibiotic is very difficult. Carbapenems (IV antibiotics like ertapenem or meropenem) are the only reliable treatment for ESBL infections — this is a serious public health crisis requiring urgent action on antimicrobial stewardship.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the most important thing to do for pyelonephritis at home?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Three essential things: (1) Complete the full antibiotic course exactly as prescribed — even when you feel better within 48-72 hours, bacteria may persist in the kidney and stopping early risks relapse and resistance; (2) Drink plenty of fluids — minimum 2.5-3 litres of water and fluids daily; high urine flow physically flushes bacteria from the urinary tract and maintains kidney perfusion; (3) Monitor temperature twice daily and watch for warning signs — if fever does not improve within 48-72 hours of antibiotics, or if you develop confusion, severe worsening of symptoms, or inability to pass urine — go to emergency department immediately. Paracetamol is safe for fever; avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen) if you are dehydrated or your kidney function may be affected.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I keep getting kidney infections — is there anything I can do to prevent them?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — recurrent UTI and pyelonephritis are largely preventable. The most evidence-based measures are: (1) Drink 2.5-3 litres of water daily — high urine flow is the single most important prevention strategy; (2) Urinate after sexual intercourse (within 15-30 minutes) — flushes bacteria from the urethra; (3) Change contraception method if using spermicides or a diaphragm — these disrupt the protective vaginal Lactobacillus flora significantly; (4) Take D-mannose supplement (2g daily) — competes with E. coli for uroepithelial binding receptors; RCT evidence comparable to antibiotic prophylaxis; (5) Eat daily plain yogurt (dahi) or take Lactobacillus probiotics — restore protective vaginal and gut flora; (6) For post-menopausal women — vaginal oestrogen cream prescribed by GP; (7) Ask GP about low-dose preventive antibiotics (trimethoprim 100mg nightly) if all the above fail. Also investigate for: diabetes, VUR, incomplete bladder emptying, and urological abnormalities.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is nitrofurantoin (Macrobid/Furadantin) safe to take for a kidney infection?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: NO — nitrofurantoin should NEVER be used for pyelonephritis (kidney infection). This is a critically important distinction. Nitrofurantoin achieves very high concentrations in the urine but does NOT achieve adequate concentrations in the kidney tissue or bloodstream — it is effective only for lower urinary tract infections (cystitis — bladder infection). Using nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis will appear to improve urinary symptoms temporarily but will fail to eradicate bacteria from the kidney, risking relapse, complications, and antibiotic resistance. Nitrofurantoin is appropriate ONLY for uncomplicated cystitis (lower UTI) and as prophylaxis for recurrent UTI — not for treatment of kidney infection.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How long will it take to recover from pyelonephritis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: For uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a healthy young woman: fever typically resolves within 48-72 hours of starting appropriate antibiotics; urinary symptoms (burning, frequency) improve within 24-48 hours; loin pain typically resolves within 3-5 days; general fatigue and malaise can persist for 2-4 weeks even after all other symptoms resolve — this is normal. Antibiotic course is typically 7 days (for fluoroquinolones) or 10-14 days (for beta-lactams). You should feel progressively better from day 2-3 of antibiotics — if not improving, contact your doctor. Complete the full course even if feeling well earlier. Return to normal activities when fever-free for 48 hours. More complex cases (abscess, sepsis, ESBL organisms) may require 4-6 weeks of antibiotics and much longer clinical recovery.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My child had a kidney infection — what tests should be done to check for underlying problems?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: After a febrile UTI in a child, investigations for underlying structural abnormalities are important — particularly vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) which causes recurrent pyelonephritis and permanent renal scarring. Current NICE UK guidance recommends: (1) Renal ultrasound in all children after febrile UTI — checks kidney size, scarring, and collecting system; (2) DMSA scintigraphy scan at 4-6 months after acute infection — the most sensitive test to detect renal cortical scarring; (3) Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) — detects vesicoureteric reflux; recommended for all boys after first UTI and girls after a second UTI or with ultrasound abnormality. Antibiotic prophylaxis (low-dose cefalexin or trimethoprim nightly) is prescribed for children with significant VUR or recurrent pyelonephritis while awaiting possible surgical correction. Long-term blood pressure monitoring and kidney function checks are needed for children with renal scarring.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I'm pregnant and have been told I have bacteria in my urine but no symptoms. Do I need treatment?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: YES — absolutely. Asymptomatic bacteriuria (bacteria in urine without symptoms) in pregnancy is a medical condition requiring antibiotic treatment, unlike in non-pregnant adults where it usually requires no treatment. In pregnancy, asymptomatic bacteriuria progresses to symptomatic UTI or pyelonephritis in 30-40% of untreated cases — putting both mother and baby at risk. This is why all pregnant women are screened with a urine culture at their booking (first) antenatal visit and often at subsequent visits. Treatment: pregnancy-safe antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefalexin, or nitrofurantoin — but NOT in the last month of pregnancy) for 3-7 days, followed by a test-of-cure urine culture 7 days after completing treatment, and repeat urine cultures at subsequent antenatal visits.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What does a 'kidney infection test' (urine test) actually show, and how accurate is it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: There are two levels of urine testing for pyelonephritis: (1) Urine dipstick (urinalysis) — a rapid 60-second test measuring leucocyte esterase (marker of white blood cells from infection — 75% sensitive) and nitrites (marker of Gram-negative bacteria reducing nitrates — 50% sensitive but very specific); combined positive result has ~90% sensitivity. A positive dipstick strongly supports UTI but does NOT identify the specific organism or antibiotic sensitivities — this is the limitation. (2) Urine culture and sensitivity (MSU) — the gold standard test; takes 24-72 hours to grow the bacteria in the laboratory and test antibiotic susceptibilities. This test tells you exactly what organism is causing the infection and which antibiotics will work. Urine culture should be sent before starting antibiotics for ALL cases of pyelonephritis — in India especially, where ESBL resistance rates are very high, knowing the organism's sensitivity is essential to choosing the correct antibiotic. White blood cell casts in urine microscopy are pathognomonic (highly specific) for pyelonephritis, confirming kidney rather than bladder involvement.
